sent_and_label: Should there be censorship in libraries?
This would have to be a mixed answer, with a little bit of both sides.
On one hand, some materials can be harmful or inappropriate for certain age groups.
On the other hand, censorship can limit freedom of speech and the diversity of ideas.
It is important to consider the age appropriateness of certain materials in libraries.
Children should not be exposed to explicit or violent content that they may not be able to fully understand.
For example, a book with graphic sexual content should not be readily available for young children to pick up.
However, there should be a system in place where parents or guardians can make the decision for their children.
A separate section for mature content or a labeling system could be implemented to help parents make informed decisions.
But censorship should not be taken too far.
Everyone has the right to access information and ideas, even if they may be controversial or offensive.
Removing materials that some may find offensive sets a dangerous precedent.
If we start censoring certain books or ideas, where do we draw the line?
Who gets to decide what is appropriate or not?
This could lead to a slippery slope where certain voices are silenced and the diversity of ideas is limited.
In my own experience, I have read books that some may find offensive or controversial, but they have challenged my own beliefs and expanded my understanding of the world.
It is important to have access to a variety of perspectives and ideas, even if we do not agree with them.
So when the question of censorship in libraries comes up you have to take all of the different angles in to mind.

One cannot simply remove something because it is offensive to some people, because that would be taking away the freedom of speech from the person who wrote it and you should never infringe upon someone's freedoms.

In the essay "Rough Road Ahead" by Joe Kurmaskie, the features of the setting affect the cyclist in many ways.
The author describes his journey through the high deserts of California during the hot summer month of June.
The lack of water, abandoned buildings, and rough terrain all contribute to the challenges the cyclist faces.
The first challenge the cyclist faces is the lack of water.
The author pumps water from a rusty pump that tastes like battery acid.
He also conserves his water as he travels towards the next town.
When he finally reaches a building, it turns out to be an abandoned Welch's Grape Juice factory.
The lack of water and the cyclist's dehydration affect his physical abilities and mindset.
The second challenge the cyclist faces is the rough terrain.
The author describes the terrain changing from flat road to short, rolling hills.
He also encounters a large snake that blocks the pavement and tumbleweeds that cross his path.
The rough terrain affects the cyclist's speed and balance.
Despite the challenges and disappointing views, the author keeps his spirits up and keeps pushing.
He breaks the ride down into distances he can see on the horizon and tells himself that if he can make it that far, he'll be fine.
He also sucks on stones to help take his mind off thirst.
In conclusion, the features of the setting in "Rough Road Ahead" affect the cyclist in many ways.
The lack of water and rough terrain contribute to the challenges the cyclist faces.
However, the author's determination and positive attitude help him overcome these challenges.
Though the author is faced with empty disappointing views, he keeps his spirits up and keeps pushing

Patience is one of the things that people need to have.
It means that you are understanding and tolerant.
You don't get angry or upset when things don't happen as quickly as you want them to.
You wait calmly and trust that everything will work out in the end.
One time, I was waiting in line at the supermarket with my cousin and her mom.
We had a lot of items, and the line was moving slowly.
My cousin was impatient that day because she wanted to go home.
She kept on whining and complaining about how she was tired and hungry, but her mom just said, "Patience is a virtue."
Then, something happened that made my cousin realize the importance of patience.
A woman in front of us in the checkout line was having trouble counting her money.
She kept dropping coins and bills, and it was taking a long time.
My cousin was getting even more impatient, but her mom told her to be patient and wait for the woman to finish.
Finally, the woman finished counting her money and left.
When it was our turn to check out, the cashier told us that the woman had paid for our items as an apology for taking so long.
My cousin was shocked and realized that if we had been impatient and left, we would have missed out on this kind act.
From that day on, my cousin learned to be more patient.
She realized that being patient means being understanding and tolerant, even when things don't go as planned.
It also means experiencing difficulties without complaining.
Patience may not always be easy, but it can lead to unexpected rewards.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One obstacle was the lack of a suitable landing area.
However, Al Smith saw an opportunity for his Empire State Building and decided to add a mooring mast to the top of the building.
This would allow dirigibles to anchor there for several hours for refueling or service, and to let passengers off and on.
The builders realized that they couldn't just set the mooring mast on top of the Empire State Building's flat roof.
If a thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, it would add stress to the building's frame.
The stress of the dirigible's load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Therefore, the steel frame of the Empire State Building had to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
Another obstacle the builders faced was the constantly shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
Also, existing laws against airships flying too low over urban areas made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
In the end, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared by the late 1930s.

Instead, the rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world's highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.
The highest open observation deck, intended for disembarking passengers, has never been open to the public.

The worker faced many obsticals while building the Empire State Building.
One of the biggest challenges was creating a mooring mast that would allow dirigibles to dock there.
The mast had to be designed so that it could support the weight of a dirigible, which could be as long as four blocks in New York City.
The architects had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the building, which cost over $60,000.
They designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
However, the builders faced many challenges when attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles when they tried to allow dirigibles to dock there.
First, they had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the building to accommodate the stress of a dirigible's load and the wind pressure that would come with it.
This cost over sixty thousand dollars.
They also had to design a mooring mast that would be safe and practical.
The mast had to be more than just a plain utilitarian structure, so the architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
One of the greatest obstacles was making the mooring mast safe.
However, there were many obstacles that prevented the mooring mast from ever fulfilling its purpose.
One reason was for safety; most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
In addition, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting, making it difficult to keep a dirigible in place.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
The other obstacle was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.
Two weeks later, another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
Because the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, a worker atop the mooring mast would have to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was abandoned.
If a dirigibles were to catch fire over a heavily populated area like New York the casualties would be numerous.
These were some of the many obstacles builders faced when attempting to construct a mooring mast on the Empire State Building.

This means that if we start censoring materials, soon there will be nothing left on the shelves for anyone to read.
Everyone has different opinions on what is offensive, so what may be offensive to one person may not be to another.
Furthermore, censorship goes against our First Amendment rights.
The First Amendment of the United States Constitution protects our freedom of speech and expression.
By censoring materials in libraries, we are limiting the free flow of information and ideas, which is essential in a democratic society.
Instead of censorship, we should encourage open dialogue and discussion.
If someone finds a book or other material offensive, they should be able to express their concerns and have a conversation about it.
This can lead to a better understanding of different perspectives and opinions.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the solution.
It limits our First Amendment rights and goes against the free flow of information and ideas.
Instead, we should encourage open dialogue and discussion about materials that may be considered offensive.

In the story, “Do not exceed postal speed limit,” many features of the setting affect the cyclist.
First and most importantly, he is affected by the people who live there.
The old-timers he met at the reservoir campground outside of Lodi, California gave him bad travel advice, causing him to take a shortcut that added hours to his ride.
They pointed out landmarks and towns that he would come across, but most of them were ghost towns or abandoned factories.
He was misled by their wisdom and keen sense of direction, which proved to be outdated.
There was no one around that he could ask for help from.
The cyclist is also affected by the terrain.
The rough and hilly roads slowed him down and made him use more energy.
He also encountered a large snake and tumbleweeds, which made his journey even more difficult.
His water supply was also affected by the terrain.
The pump he found was rusty and the water tasted like battery acid.
The cyclist was forced to conserve his water and go inward for an hour or so, which was a test of his inner spirit.
Finally, the weather affected the cyclist.
He was traveling through the high deserts of California in June, which made the heat unbearable.
The lack of shade and cool water made his journey even more difficult.
He was covered in dried sweat and was at risk of heatstroke.
In conclusion, the setting in “Do not exceed postal speed limit” affected the cyclist in many ways.
The people he encountered, the terrain he traveled on, and the weather he endured all made his journey more difficult.
The cyclist learned a valuable lesson and promised himself that he would always stick to his map in the future.

The Empire State Building is an amazing sight to see.
It stands at 1,250 feet, the tallest in New York.
At the top of the building is a mast, originally planned to be used as a mooring mast for dirigibles, also known as blimps.
The architects of the Empire State Building faced many problems with putting the mooring mast on the top of the building.
They could not simply drop a mooring mast on top of the building’s flat roof.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.

The builders were forced to, "design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself".
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate the new mooring mast.
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped, but they were unsuccessful due to forceful winds.
By the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.
The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One major issue was that dirigibles from outside the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
This became a huge safety concern after the Hindenburg disaster in 1937.
Another obstacle was that the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
Additionally, there was a law in place stating that dirigibles could not land that close to the city, which made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
It would also be nearly impossible to safely land what is essentially a balloon that close to the many buildings considering the force of the winds.
Overall, the builders should have seen that their plan for the dirigibles was entirely unrealistic.
Perhaps the largest overlooked issue was that there was a law in place stating that the dirigibles could not land that close to the city.
In spite of all these obstacles, the architects still went ahead with their plans to build the mooring mast.
They designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
Despite the elaborate design, the mooring mast was never used for its intended purpose.
The dangers of using hydrogen-filled dirigibles became too great after the Hindenburg disaster, and the winds on top of the building proved too unpredictable for safe docking.

The rooms that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.
The highest open observation deck, intended for disembarking passengers, has never been open to the public.
Such as it would be nearly impossible to safely land what is essentially a balloon that close to the many buildings considering the force of the winds.
Overall the builders should have seen that they're plan for the dirigibles was entirely unrealistic

The large highway sign warning of the rough road ahead is a reminder of the challenges he faces.

The rusty pump he encounters provides only brackish water that tastes like battery acid, leaving him with only a few tantalizing sips of water in his bottles.
He resorts to sucking on stones to take his mind off his thirst.
The abandoned Welch's Grape Juice factory is a cruel irony, as it once provided refreshment, but now offers nothing but a sandblasted picture of a young boy pouring juice into his mouth.
The cyclist's exhaustion is also intensified by the rough, hilly terrain and the warning sign of the "Rough Road Ahead."

The abandoned towns and buildings add to his sense of isolation and desperation, as he is alone in this harsh environment.
Despite these challenges, the cyclist perseveres and eventually finds relief at Gary and Wilber's fish camp.

The Empire State Building was meant to be great The tallest building in the world.
However, the Chrysler Building had a trick up its sleeve.
It secretly constructed a 185-foot spire inside the building, and then hoisted it up to the top of the Chrysler Building, making it taller than the Empire State Building.
Al Smith, the builder of the Empire State Building, announced that he would add a top or a hat to the building that would be even more distinctive than any other building in the city.
The building would now be equipped with a mooring mast at its top for docking new airships, which would accommodate passengers on transatlantic routes.
The architects could not simply drop a mooring mast on top of the Empire State Building’s flat roof.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
The back of the ship would swivel around the mooring mast, and trying to weigh it down with bricks was impractical.
Another problem that was faced was the law that would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
But two ships did try to land.
The U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles failed in landing because it was too dangerous.

The Goodyear blimp Columbia attempted a publicity stunt but the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, so a worker atop the mooring mast had to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.
In the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the biggest obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
If an accident were to happen above a densely populated area such as downtown New York, it could be disastrous.
Another obstacle was the shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if a dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Additionally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, making it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
To accommodate a dirigible, the steel frame of the building had to be modified and strengthened, costing over sixty thousand dollars.
Placing a thousand-foot dirigible moore on the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would of added pressure to the building's frame work.
Therefore, the steel frame would have to be modified and strengthed.
With all this work, over sixty thousand dollars had to be made.
Despite all the work and modifications made to the building, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had to be abandoned.
Dirigibles were not the transportation of the future, as airplanes replaced them.

The rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.
The highest open observation deck, intended for disembarking passengers, has never been open to the public.
It was very difficult building a mooring mast on the top of the Empire Building, when having tough obstacles to go through.

TAYLORSVILLE, N.C. (AP) — Where do you hide a 1,000-pound chicken?
That's what sheriff's deputies in Alexander County, North Carolina, are trying to figure out as they search for the concrete statue that disappeared from a farm west of Taylorsville over the weekend.
While the chicken may be heavy, it's only 3 feet tall.
Deputies think the statue was taken sometime between 8 p.m. Saturday and 9 a.m. Sunday from the driveway of the farm.
Chief Deputy Tod Jones told the Hickory Daily Record (http://bit.ly/2l7Z6BF) the statue's base was found several miles away.
The missing concrete bird has left the farm owners and local community puzzled and concerned.
The unique half-ton statue had become a beloved landmark in the area, attracting visitors and becoming a symbol of the farm's identity.
Authorities are urging anyone with information about the missing chicken to come forward and help solve the mystery of its disappearance.
Meanwhile, the farm owners are hopeful for the safe return of their prized concrete bird.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in trying to allow dirigibles to dock there.
The builders needed to make sure the dirigible would be light enough to go through the air.
They used ""envelopes of cotton fabric filled with hydrogen and helium to make them lighter than air.""
They had to have the dirigible go to a speed of eighty miles per hour but also to aboard and unboard passengers safely.
The mooring mast had to be designed carefully, as a thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
The biggest obstacle was safety because most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
Another obstacle was the constantly shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if a dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these weights at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Additionally, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Despite these obstacles, the builders continued to work on a practical and safe way to moor airships to the mast.
However, by the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.

Cuba has opened its first wholesale market, lending a hand to some non-state businesses in an economy dominated by government-run enterprises.
State-run newspaper Granma said the market is part of an ongoing effort to "reorganize" commerce on the communist island.
The market will sell beans, beer, sugar, cigars and other goods for 20 to 30 percent less than the products cost at state-owned retail stores throughout the country.
The wholesale market represents a significant shift in Cuba's economic landscape, offering a glimmer of hope for private businesses seeking more affordable supplies.
However, access to the market remains limited, with entry restricted to certain non-state businesses holding government licenses.
This move is seen as a cautious step towards economic liberalization in a country where the state has traditionally held a tight grip on commerce.
While the opening of the wholesale market is a positive development for some non-state businesses, many challenges remain.
Limited access and restrictions on the types of businesses allowed to purchase goods from the market highlight the complexities of Cuba's economic transition.
The success of this initiative will depend on how effectively it addresses the needs of private enterprises and contributes to a more diverse and competitive business environment.

MONTREAL — A Catholic group says it is bringing the right forearm of a 16th-century Jesuit missionary on a cross-Canada tour to celebrate the country’s 150th birthday.
The relic, believed to be that of Saint Francis Xavier, will be displayed in various cities across Canada as part of a special commemoration for the nation's milestone anniversary.
The tour will start in St. John's, Newfoundland, and make its way westward, stopping in major cities such as Halifax, Quebec City, Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary, and Vancouver.
Pilgrims and visitors will have the opportunity to view and venerate the relic, which holds significant religious and historical importance.
Saint Francis Xavier was a pioneering missionary who played a crucial role in spreading Christianity to Asia during the 16th century.
His right arm, preserved as a relic, is revered by Catholics around the world.
The tour aims to honor his legacy and celebrate Canada's rich history and cultural diversity.
The Catholic group organizing the tour hopes that bringing the relic to different communities will inspire faith, unity, and reflection on the country's past and future.
The tour is set to culminate in a special ceremony in Ottawa, the nation's capital, to mark the conclusion of the celebrations for Canada's 150th birthday.

The Empire State Building was originally designed to be the tallest building in the world, and the builders wanted to make it even more distinctive by adding a mooring mast at the top for docking dirigibles or zeppelins.
However, there were several obstacles that the architects and engineers had to overcome.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is a highly flammable product.
The owners of the Empire State Building realized that if a dirigible caught fire above a densely populated area such as downtown New York, it could cause a lot of damage.
Another obstacle was the shifting winds on top of the building, which made it difficult to moor a dirigible safely.
Even if a dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast, and it would be dangerous to use lead weights to anchor it down.
Additionally, there was a law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which would make it illegal for a dirigible to tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Finally, by the late 1930s, airplanes had replaced dirigibles as the transportation of the future, and the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.

The majestic spire of the empire State Building is familiar to many people throghout the world, but not many know that the original purpose of the mast was to serve as a landing spot for dirigibles, also know as blimps.
The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the biggest problems was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
The other major obstacle was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Therefore, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared by the late 1930s.

Two officers testified Tuesday that Maxwell Morton, then 16, showed little emotion or concern about the February 2015 shooting of 16-year-old Ryan Mangan.
Westmoreland County Detective James Williams told jurors "when he described pulling the trigger, he had a little smirk on his face."

Police contend Morton took a photograph of himself with Mangan's body minutes after the shooting and an hour later sent the image via Snapchat while he played online video games with a teen in Wisconsin.
The prosecution argued that Morton's actions were callous and demonstrated a lack of remorse for the heinous crime he committed.
Morton's defense attorney, however, claimed that his client was in a state of shock and did not fully comprehend the gravity of his actions at the time.
The trial is expected to delve into Morton's mental state and intentions leading up to and following the tragic incident.
As the trial progresses, more details are likely to emerge regarding the events that led to the shooting and Morton's behavior in the aftermath.
Stay tuned for further updates as the case unfolds.

Access Power, a leading developer, and operator of power projects in emerging markets, has announced the launch of the Access Co-Development Facility (ACF) 2018, offering a clean power prize to innovative renewable energy projects.
The ACF is a competition that aims to identify and support local power project developers in Africa and, for the first time, in Asia.
The initiative seeks to provide financial support, technical expertise, and access to the right partnerships to help bring pioneering renewable energy projects to life.
Access Power is specifically looking for projects that can demonstrate significant potential to make a positive impact on their communities while promoting clean energy solutions.
In three years, the ACF has considered a total of 234 projects for the prize, Access said.
Finalists for ACF 2018, which covers Asia for the first time, will be evaluated and scored by an independent panel of industry experts, with the three winners announced in June.
The winners will then enter into direct joint development agreement (JDA) discussions with Access Power.
Interested parties have until 10 May to apply for consideration.

County Judge Aurelio Guerra says the new lockup will boost the local economy.
The decision to repurpose the site of the former prison, which was shuttered after the riot, has sparked mixed reactions among residents and advocacy groups.
Supporters of the new immigration lockup highlight the economic benefits it will bring to the struggling community, providing job opportunities and potential revenue for local businesses.
However, critics express concerns about the impact on immigrant detainees' rights and the history of issues related to the previous facility.
The construction and operation of the new facility are expected to take several months, with plans to address security measures and living conditions for detainees.
As discussions continue on the implications of this development, the community remains divided on the future of the immigration lockup in Willacy County.

There are many obstacles the builders of the Empire State building faced in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
one issue was the stress the dirigible would add to the building.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Also, most dirigibles contained hydrogen which is highly flammable and dangerouss.
Another dangerous aspect is that this huge piece of material would be dangling high above pedestrians, as opposed to there much safer usual landing of open fields.
Lastly, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which would also cause docking issues.

The dirigibles were not able to dock on the mast of the Empire State Building for obvious reasons.
When the construction workers were building the mast, they didn't realize how dangerous it was having a dirigible landing on the top of the building.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Another practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.

In the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared, and the rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.

She has vowed to continue her work as the head of the Supreme Court, challenging the government's attempts to undermine the rule of law in Poland.

HONOLULU (AP) — A Hawaii emergency management official who said last week that his retirement had nothing to do with a mistaken missile alert that stirred panic statewide now says it was because of the fallout from the warning.
The former administrator, Vern Miyagi, had initially claimed that his departure was unrelated to the false missile alert issued in January.
However, in a recent interview, Miyagi admitted that the intense scrutiny and criticism following the incident were significant factors in his decision to resign.
The false alarm, which warned residents and tourists of an incoming ballistic missile and urged them to seek immediate shelter, caused widespread panic and confusion across Hawaii.
Investigations into the incident revealed that the alert was sent in error during a routine test of the emergency alert system.
The mistake highlighted flaws in the state's emergency preparedness protocols and raised concerns about the reliability of the system.
Miyagi, who had been at the helm of Hawaii's emergency management agency for several years, faced mounting pressure to be held accountable for the false alert.
His decision to step down underscores the serious repercussions of the erroneous warning and the need for improved safeguards to prevent similar incidents in the future.>

VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. (AP) – Macon Brock, a retailer who co-founded the Dollar Tree chain of discount stores that grew into a Fortune 500 company, has died.
Brock's passing marks the end of an era for the retail industry, as he played a pivotal role in revolutionizing the concept of dollar stores.
Brock, along with his partners, opened the first Dollar Tree store in 1986 in Norfolk, Virginia.
Their vision of providing quality goods at a fixed price resonated with customers, leading to the rapid expansion of the chain across the United States.
Under Brock's leadership, Dollar Tree became a household name, known for its wide array of products priced at just one dollar.
His commitment to offering affordable items while maintaining high standards of quality helped shape the company's success and enduring popularity.
The legacy of Macon Brock will be remembered not only in the business world but also in the hearts of countless customers who benefited from his innovative retail concept.

The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.

There were many obstacles that the builders of the Empire State Building faced in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.

According to the author, "... was destined to never fulfill its purpose [Empire State building being a dock for dirigibles], for reasons that should have been apparent before it was ever constructed."
As the author points out, there were many problems with this idea.
For one, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
This was a serious obstacle to mooring dirigibles.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Another obstacle was that most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Lastly, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped, but they faced problems with forceful winds and the lack of complete dirigible mooring equipment.

In the end, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared, and the rooms that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.

Everyone has the right to express themselves and share their ideas, even if we don't agree with them.
When we start censoring books, music, movies, and other materials, we limit our own freedom to read, listen, and watch what we want.
What may be offensive to one person may not be offensive to another, so who gets to decide what is censored?
It's not fair to let a small group of people make decisions for everyone else.
Additionally, censorship can prevent us from learning about different perspectives and ideas.
It's important to be exposed to different viewpoints, even if we don't agree with them.
This helps us to become more open-minded and tolerant of others.
Instead of censoring, we should focus on educating ourselves and our children about different ideas and perspectives.
We can choose not to read or watch something if we find it offensive, but we shouldn't prevent others from having access to it.

In a bizarre turn of events, Apple finds itself in an ironic situation as a memo warning employees against leaking information has, ironically, been leaked.
The memo, intended to reinforce Apple's strict policies regarding confidentiality and the protection of trade secrets, was circulated internally but somehow found its way into the public domain.
Apple's emphasis on secrecy is well-known, with the tech giant famously guarding its upcoming products and innovations with utmost vigilance.
The leaked memo serves as a stark reminder to employees of the consequences of breaching this trust and the potential impact on Apple's competitive edge in the market.
However, this incident raises questions about the effectiveness of Apple's internal communication protocols and the challenges of maintaining confidentiality in today's interconnected world.
It also highlights the delicate balance between transparency and secrecy that companies like Apple must navigate in an era where information spreads rapidly and uncontrollably.
That said, it’s hard to see leaks as entirely bad.

Although leaks do rob Apple of the opportunity for big reveals and cut into sales of older products due for replacement, Apple does benefit from the non-stop drumbeat of rumors and speculation fueled by the leaks.
Plus, while it’s entirely reasonable for Apple to want to control what is announced, it’s somewhat troubling when the company plays favorites with who is anointed with early or special access.
Also, people leak information for a variety of reasons, including self-importance and the thrill of sharing a secret.
But leaks can also happen when employees feel that the company is being overly and unnecessarily secretive.

TRAVIS AIR FORCE BASE, Calif. (AP) — A mistaken report of a shooter prompted the lockdown of Travis Air Force Base in California on Wednesday in the midst of an emergency training exercise, officials said.
The base ordered people to shelter in place and lock their doors and windows.
Gates were closed for more than an hour before the all-clear was given at the site 45 miles northeast of San Francisco .
"There were reports of gunshots at the Base Exchange.
However, no shooter was found," a base Facebook posting reported.
"There was a security exercise underway at the base and somebody took that to be an active shooter and they went from there," said U.S. Rep. John Garamendi, who was briefed on the situation.
The mistaken report led to a significant response from law enforcement agencies, including the Fairfield Police Department and the FBI.
Emergency personnel swiftly arrived on the scene to assess and address the situation.
The base’s security forces conducted a thorough search of the area to ensure there was no actual threat present.
Although the incident turned out to be a false alarm, it highlighted the importance of clear communication during emergency situations.
Base officials emphasized the need for personnel to be vigilant and follow security protocols, especially during training exercises, to prevent such misunderstandings in the future.
The lockdown was lifted, and operations at Travis Air Force Base resumed back to normal following the security scare.

Global warming might not be caused by carbon dioxide emissions after all – in fact a Danish physicist thinks changes in the earth’s climate are being caused by fluctuations in solar activity.
This controversial theory has sparked a new wave of discussions among scientists and policymakers alike.
Dr. Henrik Svensmark, a researcher at the Danish National Space Institute, has put forth the idea that cosmic rays from outer space play a significant role in shaping the earth's climate.
According to Svensmark, these cosmic rays interact with the earth's atmosphere, leading to the formation of cloud cover.
This cloud cover, in turn, affects the amount of sunlight reaching the earth's surface, ultimately influencing global temperatures.
While Svensmark's theory challenges the widely accepted view that carbon dioxide emissions are the primary driver of climate change, it has gained traction among some in the scientific community.
Proponents of this cosmic theory argue that it provides a more comprehensive explanation for the earth's climate variations throughout history.
Critics, however, remain skeptical, pointing to the overwhelming body of evidence linking human activities to rising global temperatures.
They argue that while solar activity may play a role in climate fluctuations, it is unlikely to fully account for the rapid and unprecedented warming observed in recent decades.

As the debate continues, one thing remains clear – understanding the complexities of climate change requires a multidisciplinary approach that considers a wide range of factors, both terrestrial and cosmic.>

The company doesn't go into to too much detail about what the fingerprinting involves, but it stems from a command filtering patent.
For the Super Bowl ad and other promos where Amazon already knows what's coming, Amazon will send fingerprints in advance so Alexa can compare input and ignore requests from ads.
In situations where Amazon can't predict what will happen (such as a TV segment), it uses dynamic fingerprinting that looks for many simultaneous activations based on the same audio.
This won't catch every false request, but it typically stops "80 to 90 percent" of devices from responding.
Let's put it this way -- a funny incident shouldn't devolve into national chaos.
Amazon has another technique where it can send an inaudible signal in the 3kHz to 6kHz range to stop Alexa from responding, although that doesn't appear to be in use here.
The tech giant’s move to ensure Alexa remains calm during the Super Bowl ad reflects the ongoing efforts to enhance user experience and prevent unintended activation of smart devices.
With the increasing integration of voice assistants in daily life, maintaining control over when they respond is crucial to avoid disruptions and protect user privacy.
Amazon's proactive approach to managing Alexa's responses demonstrates a commitment to addressing potential challenges in a rapidly evolving technological landscape.
By leveraging sophisticated techniques like fingerprinting and signal modulation, Amazon aims to strike a balance between convenience and security in the realm of voice-controlled devices.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
The first obstacle was that the building was not originally designed with a mooring mast, so the architects had to modify the building's framework to accommodate it.
The builders second obstacle was that they couldn't find a way to get the mooring mast on top of the building.
The builders would need to make a stronger building frame so the mast could safely be on the top of the building without adding stress to the frame.
Another obstacle that the builders faced was nature.
The wind at the top of the building was very unpredictable and strong at times.
The back of the dirigible would move from the wind, even if it was tied to the building.
This made it difficult for passengers to get on and off the dirigible safely.
Additionally, most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
This made it unsafe for dirigibles to dock at the Empire State Building, especially above densely populated areas like downtown New York.
Finally, an existing law prohibited airships from flying too low over urban areas, making it illegal for a ship to tie up to the building or even approach the area.

In a recent development concerning the tragic sinking of the cargo ship El Faro during Hurricane Joaquin in 2015, a former sailor has provided testimony that raises questions about the ship's safety protocols.
The testimony was given by former crew member Mitchell Hearman during a Coast Guard hearing investigating the incident.
Hearman recounted harrowing details of the ship's final hours, highlighting concerns about the vessel's seaworthiness and the decision-making process onboard.
He described a lack of communication from the ship's owner, Tote Services Inc., regarding the impending danger posed by the approaching hurricane.

According to Hearman, the company prioritized fuel efficiency over crew safety, as managers frequently instructed captains to slow down to conserve fuel but failed to warn them about the severe weather conditions they were sailing into.

This testimony sheds light on potential shortcomings in the safety procedures and communication practices aboard the El Faro, raising important questions about the responsibilities of ship owners and operators in ensuring the well-being of their crew members.
The revelations from Hearman's testimony may have significant implications for the ongoing investigation into the El Faro tragedy.
Hearman testified that Tote Services Inc. managers often called the ship to tell captains to slow down and conserve fuel, but didn't call to warn the crew they were headed into a strong hurricane.
In a statement, Tote spokesman Darrell Wilson said the company disagrees strongly with Hearman's testimony and is committed to supporting the lost sailors' families.

VICTORIA — Former British Columbia premier Dave Barrett has died at the age of 87.
A statement from Premier John Horgan’s office says the former NDP premier died after a long struggle with Alzheimer’s disease.
Barrett served as the premier of British Columbia from 1972 to 1975, leading the province's first New Democratic Party government.
He was known for his progressive policies aimed at addressing social inequality and improving working conditions for British Columbians.
During his time in office, Barrett implemented a range of reforms, including labor law changes, the establishment of the Agricultural Land Reserve, and the introduction of public auto insurance.
Born in Vancouver in 1930, Barrett began his political career as a social worker before entering provincial politics.
He was a charismatic and passionate leader who advocated for the rights of workers and marginalized communities.
Barrett's legacy continues to be felt in British Columbia, where his government's policies laid the foundation for many of the social programs and initiatives still in place today.
Barrett's passing has elicited an outpouring of tributes from political leaders and citizens alike, who remember him as a dedicated public servant and a champion of social justice.
He will be remembered for his contributions to the province and his commitment to making life better for all British Columbians.

KEY WEST, Fla. (AP) — Authorities say two men have been arrested in the 2010 theft of a museum's 17th-century gold bar, valued at $550,000.

A U.S. Department of Justice statement says 41-year-old Richard Steven Johnson, of Rio Linda, California, and 32-year-old Jarred Alexander Goldman, of Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, were arrested Monday and charged with conspiring to steal and stealing the gold bar from the Mel Fisher Maritime Heritage Museum in Key West.
It wasn't known if they have lawyers.
The 74.8-ounce (2.1-kilogram) bar was found in 1980 on a 1622 Spanish galleon wreck off the Florida Keys by the late shipwreck salvor Mel Fisher.
Authorities say it hasn't been recovered.
The theft of the gold bar in 2010 had puzzled investigators for years until recent developments led to the arrests of Johnson and Goldman.
The gold bar, which holds historical significance and substantial monetary value, has been a prized artifact at the Mel Fisher Maritime Heritage Museum.
The museum is known for its collection of treasures salvaged from shipwrecks in the area.
The community is eager for updates on the investigation and hopes for the safe return of the stolen gold bar.

The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.

Another problem caused by winds is the fact that the dirigible might crash into other buildings, causing, the fabric containing the hydrogen gas to be punctured, and the dirigible to crash.
In the end, it was a project deemed too risky to continue.

Another obstacle was that the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

The idea of building a dock for dirigibles was good for the time but it had several obstacles.
The first was that the moored dirigible would add stress to the buildings frame.
The stress of the dirigible's load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
Furthermore, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
This would make it unsafe for the passengers getting on and off.
It would be unsafe for the pedestrians far below as well because to control the sway weights would have to dangle from the back, as in an open landing field.
Moreover, most dirigibles from outside the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, as opposed to helium, which is safer.
This made it risky to moor the dirigibles above a densely populated area like downtown New York.
Additionally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Despite the modifications made to the building's framework and the design of the mast, the idea of using it for dirigibles was abandoned due to safety concerns and practical reasons.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and this would have been very dangerous in a densely populated area like downtown New York.

The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, so even if the dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.
This made it difficult to safely dock the dirigible.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Finally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

Traffic apps like Waze and Google Maps might be making traffic worse.
By Robert Sanders at the University of California Berkeley 2.
Could there be a treatment for the social deficits related to autism?
By Ellen Goldbaum at the University at Buffalo 3.
In a surprising turn of events, it seems that the very technology designed to help us navigate through traffic may actually be exacerbating congestion issues.

The convenience of real-time traffic updates and alternative route suggestions provided by popular navigation apps like Waze and Google Maps seems to be leading to increased traffic volume on smaller, residential roads.
Studies have shown that these apps are diverting drivers away from main thoroughfares onto quieter streets, causing unexpected traffic jams and safety concerns for local residents.
While the intention of these apps is to help users save time and avoid traffic, their widespread use may be unintentionally contributing to the problem they aim to solve.
As cities grapple with growing traffic challenges, a more holistic approach to traffic management that considers the broader impact of navigation apps may be necessary.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
They had to modify and strengthen the building's steel frame to accommodate the stress of a dirigible's load and wind pressure.
They also had to design a mooring mast that would transmit the stress all the way to the building's foundation, which was almost 1,100 feet below.
The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
So the builders constructed a huge stainless steel enclosure to house passengers.
this enclosure also had an elevator and stairs to bring passengers to the eighty fifth floor.
However, the greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

One obstacle that the builders faced when attempting to allow dirigibles to dock at the Empire State Building was, "the lack of a suitable landing area."
New York City is full of buildings and there is not a lot a flat ground to land a dirigible.

To solve this issue, the builders decided to add a mooring mast to the top of the building, which would allow dirigibles to anchor there for several hours for refueling or service, and to let passengers off and on.
However, the builders faced many obstacles in making this plan a reality.
The greatest reason why the mooring mast was never used was one of safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in New Jersey, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Another obstacle that the builders faced was nature.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

In the excerpt "The Mooring Mast" author Marcia Amidon Lüted speaks of the obsticles that the builders of the Empire State Building faced in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
First, the frame of the Building had not been built to withstand a thousand foot long blimp docking to it.
The stress of the dirigible's weight and wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework to accommodate this new situation.

Second, the architects had to design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
Lastly, the greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several challenges in building a dock for dirigibles They would not be able to simply place of mooring mast on the flat roof of the Empire State Building.
The thousand-foot dirigible held by a single cable would make the frame very unsturdy.
With the weight of the dirigible and the wind pressure it would have to get transmitted to eleven hundred feet, where the foundation is.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework to accommodate this new situation.
Also, the law that airships flying too low over urban areas would have made it illegal.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Two dirigibles attempted to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
Another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
The papers were delivered, but after this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.
By the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.

While designing and building the mooring mast atop the Empire State building, architects and builders faced many obstacles.
One of the few obstacles they noticed pre-construction was that the weight and pressure of the blimp would add stress to the frame of the building.
This meant that the steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate the stress of the dirigible's load and wind pressure.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
Additionally, the architects could not simply drop a mooring mast on top of the Empire State Building’s flat roof.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.

Rather than building a utilitarian mast without any ornamentation, the architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
However, the greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Most dirigibles outside of the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
This made it dangerous to have a dirigible docked above a densely populated area like downtown New York.
Additionally, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas also made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
The winds forced the builders to reinforce the steel frame so the load of the blimp would not tear part of the building off.
The blimp would sway in the wind making it less safe for passengers to board and depart.
The wind could blow the blimps into the spires puncturing them.
If the blimp ever ignited then the debris would fall to the crowded streets below.
The builders faced so many obstacles that when they were finished they realize how unsafe the idea really was.

The dream of the aviation pioneers of docking their dirigibles on the Empire State Building, created obstacles for the builders to face.

Firstly, the steel frame of the building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate the stress of the dirigible’s load and wind pressure, which would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.

Secondly, the architects had to design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
It was difficult for the dirigibles to dock.
The back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast, making it dangerous.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.

I think that it is wrong to remove a book or any other reading material for approprianness.
Everyone has the right to read what they want, and censorship takes away that right.
Censorship is when someone decides that certain books, music, movies, magazines, or other materials are offensive and should be removed from the shelves.
But who decides what is offensive and what is not?
What is offensive to one person may not be offensive to another.
Some people might find a book about a controversial topic like abortion or gay marriage offensive, while others might find it informative and helpful.
If we start removing books that some people find offensive, we might end up removing all the books from the shelves.
Furthermore, censorship can limit our knowledge and understanding of the world.
If we only read books that are approved by someone else, we might miss out on important information and ideas.
We might not be able to learn about different cultures, religions, or lifestyles.
We might not be able to form our own opinions and ideas.
In conclusion, censorship is wrong because it takes away our right to read what we want and limits our knowledge and understanding of the world.
We should have the freedom to read what we want without someone else deciding what is appropriate for us.
As Katherine Paterson said, if we start removing books from the shelves, we might end up with no books left for any of us.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One obsticle they faced was the fact that the building was not strong enough to hold the giant dirigibles.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
Another obstacle was the fact that most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.

"Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe."
Another obstacle was the wind on top of the building, which was constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles attempted to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
However, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared by the late 1930s.

Dirigibles are enormous steel framed balloons with envelopes of cotton fabric filled with hydrogen and helium.
The biggest obstacle was when the dirigible would be moored to the building it would cause a lot of stress.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
Another obstacle was that most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.

Today, I would like to talk about censorship in libraries.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
But is censorship really the answer?
As Katherine Paterson, author of "Bridge to Terabithia," said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This means that if we start censoring books, music, and movies that we find offensive, then soon there will be nothing left for anyone to read, listen to, or watch.
Instead of censoring, we should trust our children to make their own decisions about what they want to read or watch.
We should encourage them to read books that challenge them and help them grow as individuals.
We should also talk to them about the things they are watching and listening to, and help them understand why certain things may not be appropriate for their age.
