The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles while attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.

They had to make sure that the building could withstand the stress from the dirigible's load and wind pressure, which would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, nearly eleven hundred feet below.
They also had to make sure it could stand the wind currents.
After all that hard work, Al Smith had a bigger idea.Al Smith wanted to make the mooring mast at the top of the Empire State Building, a place where dirigibles could anchor for several hours.
He also thought that it would be a good place for the dirigles to get fueling if needed and it would be an opportunity for the passengers to get on & off the dirigibles for a break.
Unfortunately for Al Smith, the Plan didn't work.
The builders faced many obstacles when it came to the safety of the dirigibles.
Most dirigibles from outside the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Another obstacle was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
One of the moods in the memoir was greatful.
The author, Narciso Rodriguez, expressed his gratitude towards his parents for their love and sacrifice.
He mentioned that his parents came to the United States with courage and without any knowledge of the language or the culture.
They struggled both personally and financially, braving the harsh northern winters while yearning for their native tropics and facing cultural hardships.
Despite these difficulties, they worked hard to give their children a better life.
The author acknowledged that what his parents did was much more courageous than he could have ever done, and he admired their strength and perseverance.
The memoir also created a warm and loving mood.
Rodriguez described his childhood home as a traditional Cuban home, where the heart of the house was the kitchen.
His parents shared cooking duties, and their rich culinary skills and love of cooking were passed on to him.
Passionate Cuban music filled the air, mixing with the aromas of the kitchen.
The author's childhood was filled with innocence, family, and friends, and endless celebrations that encompassed both.

Despite living in a neighborhood made up of mostly Spanish, Cuban, and Italian immigrants at a time when overt racism was the norm and segregation prevailed in the United States, all of these cultures came together in great solidarity and friendship.
It was a close-knit community of honest, hardworking immigrants who extended a hand to people who, while not necessarily their own kind, were clearly in need.
In conclusion, the memoir Home: The Blueprints of Our Lives -- Written by Narciso Rodriguez, created a grateful, warm, and loving mood.
The author expressed his gratitude towards his parents for their love and sacrifice and acknowledged the courage and strength they had to endure the hardships of living in a new country.
The memoir also depicted the warm and loving environment of the author's childhood home, where family, friends, and celebrations were the heart of the house.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock on the building.
One obstacle was that there was "an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas."
This made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Another reason was because of safety.
Hydrogen is used by many dirigibles from outside the U.S.
This is not safe because hydrogen is highly flammable unlike helium.
In the article it states, "Most dirigibles from outside of the United States use hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable."
This is an obstacle because there have been accidents in the past that involve a dirigible being destroyed by a fire.
No one wants to let an accident like that occur again.
Another obstacle that the builders faced was nature.
Due to the "violent air currents" if a dirigible were tethered to the morning mast it would cause problems.
This would cause the back of the ship to swivel around the mooring mast.
the author writes, "where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe."
The dirigible would not be safe in New York.

The captain of the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles could not even take his hands off the control levers because of forceful winds.
The architects and engineers of the Empire State Building had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the building to accommodate the mooring mast.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The mooring mast had a skeleton of steel and was clad in stainless steel with glass windows.
Two months after the workers celebrated framing the entire building, they were back to raise an American flag again—this time at the top of the frame for the mooring mast.

The idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared by the late 1930s.

People should have the right to choose what they want to read, watch, or listen to.
If someone wants to read a book that may be offensive to others, they should be allowed to do so.
It is up to the individual to decide what is appropriate for them.

The environment around people in certain situations can affect them in many ways.
In the essay "Rough Road Ahead" by Joe Kurmaskie, the cyclist is affected by the setting of the high deserts of California.
He is on a solo ride to Yosemite National Park, but he takes the wrong path following the advice of some old-timers.
As he rides on, he encounters "ghost towns," "rolling hills," and "tumbleweeds."
He also faces extreme heat, dehydration, and a lack of water.
These features of the setting make his journey much harder than he anticipated.
The cyclist's thirst is a major issue throughout the essay.
He encounters a rusted water pump that gives him brackish water that tastes like battery acid.
He also comes across an abandoned Welch's Grape Juice factory, which only adds to his desperation.
The terrain he faces is also a challenge.
He encounters a sign that warns of a "rough road ahead" and is only doing 12 mph on a highway where the speed limit is 55 mph.
He also sees a large snake, which adds to his fear and thirst.
Despite these challenges, the cyclist is also affected positively by the setting.
He is surrounded by "cool pines and rushing rivers" that make him feel at peace.
He also notes that the "world is a fluid place" and that things can change.
This realization helps him to keep going and to not give up.
In the end, he finds a fish camp where he can replenish his water supply and continue on his journey.
In this cyclist case the environment affected him in many ways, from bumpy roads, “ghost towns, and trees.
For example he said, “The sun was beginning to beat down, but I barley noticed,” this is because of the "cool pines" around him as he explains in the next paragraph.
It also says in the text that the terrain changed and he even came upon a snake, which added to his thirst.
So then making it harder for him to go one.
From reading the the text on can see how features can have effects on a person.

He tried again and again, but it just wasn't working.
Finally, he got frustrated and decided to give up.
He stood up and started to walk away, but then he slipped on the wet sand and fell right into the ocean!

After he got out of the water, we all helped him clean up and get the sand out of his hair.

That day showed me just how important laughter is.
Even when things don't go the way we planned, we can still find joy in the moment and share that joy with others.
Laughter brings people together and helps us forget our worries for a little while.
Without laughter, life would be a lot less fun.

In the story "Winter Hibiscus" by Minfong Ho, Saeng is a teenage girl who has recently moved from Vietnam to the United States with her family.
Saeng is struggling to adjust to her new life and feels homesick for her old country.
When she sees a hibiscus plant at a florist shop, it reminds her of her childhood in Vietnam and brings her comfort.
However, she also feels overwhelmed by the unfamiliarity of her new surroundings and misses her grandmother and the familiar things from her childhood.
At the end of the story, Saeng vows to retake her driving test in the spring, after the snow melts and the geese return, and the hibiscus plant is budding again.
This symbolizes her willingness to start over and make a new life for herself in her new country.

Saeng has come to realize that while she misses her old home, she has also grown accustomed to the new things around her, like the bitter melon her mother cooks and the sound of the Canada geese flying overhead.
Saeng's decision to retake the driving test in the spring shows that she is ready to embrace her new life and make the most of the opportunities available to her.
She has come to accept that her new home is where she lives now and is willing to work hard to make it feel like home.
The hibiscus plant represents a connection to Saeng's past, but also a symbol of hope for her future.
She knows that she can't go back to her old life, but she can create a new one for herself in this new, familiar country.
In conclusion, Saeng's vow to retake her driving test in the spring represents her willingness to start over and make a new life for herself in her new country.
She has come to accept her new surroundings and is ready to embrace the opportunities available to her.
The hibiscus plant reminds her of her past but also symbolizes hope for her future.
She’s saying that once the hibiscus is budding and the geese return, she can start over.
She is willing to start a new life in her new world.
The whole story is talking about how upset she is about being in a new country, missing her grandmother, and missing everything else about her childhood.
When she sees the plant from her childhood country, it brings comfort to see something that means something to her.
She gets upset though because she sees how out of place she is in this new country and how she wishes she were in her childhood again.
When she gets home and shows the plant to her mother, she realizes that things in this new country have also become familiar to her.
She knows that this is where she lives now and she can set things right in this new, Familiar country.
She’s saying that once she is fully ready and understands her new home, she’ll be ready to take the driving test and start a new life.

In the memoir "Home: The Blueprints of Our Lives" by Narciso Rodriguez, the author creates a mood of compassion.
He describes his childhood home, which was a modest, three-room apartment in the Ironbound section of Newark, New Jersey.
Despite the challenging circumstances of his parents' immigrant experience, the author recalls the warmth of his home and the love that was shared within its walls.
The kitchen was the heart of the home, where his parents shared cooking duties and passed on their rich culinary skills to him.
Cuban music filled the air, mixing with the aromas of the kitchen, creating a joyful and welcoming atmosphere.
The author grew up in a close-knit community of honest, hardworking immigrants who extended a hand to people in need.
His parents welcomed everyone into their home, and the air was always filled with "not just scent and music but life and love."
The author learned the importance of family and friends from his parents, who showed him with their lives the spirit of generosity and perseverance.
These teachings became the basis of his life.
The author's memoir is full of gratitude and admiration for his parents' strength and sacrifice.
He learned what family really meant and learned how to love.
The author's parents came to the United States with courage and selflessness, leaving behind their families, friends, and careers to give their children a better life.
The author's parents endured many hardships, but their faith in a better future drove them to persevere.
In conclusion, the memoir "Home: The Blueprints of Our Lives" by Narciso Rodriguez creates a mood of compassion.
The author's recollections of his childhood home and the love shared within its walls demonstrate the importance of family and friends.
He learned generosity and how important family and friends are from his parents and they have been "the basis" of his life.
His house welcomed everyone and the air was always filled with "not just scent and music but life and love.
He learned what family really ment and learned how to love.
He loved his parents a lot and talked highly of them in his memoir "My mother and father had come to this country with such courage, without any knowledge of the language or the culture.
They came selflessly, as many immigrants do, to give their children a better life, even though it meant leaving behind their families, friends, and careers in the country they love...
The faith that this struggle would lead them and their children to better times drove them to endure these hard times."
That is why I think that the mood in the memoir "Narciso Rodriguez from Home: The Blueprints of our lives" is compassion.

When the Empire State Building was being constructed, the builders faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
The first problem was that a dirigible moored at the top of the building would add stress to the building's frame.
The stress of the dirigible's load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
Another obstacle was the safety of the dirigibles.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
This was a major concern, especially after the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937.
The owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
The winds on top of the building were also constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Lastly, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped, the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed.

The Empire State Building was built as the tallest building in the World and even today still remains one of the tallest.
It had design plans with more of a purpose then just being the tallest building, however.
It was supposed to serve as a passenger exchange and a refueling dock for dirigibles.
Most people do not know this though because there were many complications involved with the architectural designs of this plan for the mast.
Architects knew it would not be easy to build such a creation and that they "could not simply drop a mooring mast on top of the Empire State Building."
One of the main obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and if an accident were to happen above a densely populated area such as downtown New York, it would be catastrophic.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
An existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas was also a problem.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
The U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.
Two weeks later, another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
Because the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, a worker atop the mooring mast would have to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles and attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
They could not simply drop a mooring mast on the flat roof of the Empire State Building.
A thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top of the building, held by a single cable tether, would add stress to the building’s frame.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
However, the greatest reason why the mooring mast was never used was one of safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas also made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
The height of the Mast also made it much too windy for docking.

Irving Clavan from the building's architectural office said, ""The yet unsolved problems of mooring airships to a fix mast at such a height made it desirable to postpone to a later date the final installation of landing gear.""
This never did happen and the mast went unused.

In the essay “Rough Road Ahead” by Joe Kurmaskie, the setting features greatly affect the cyclist and his well-being.
The cyclist is traveling through the high deserts of California in June, where the terrain is changing, and the weather is hot.
This affects the cyclist’s physical state, as he is dehydrated and exhausted due to the lack of water and the sun beating down on him.
The cyclist is also affected mentally as he begins to lose hope and becomes desperate for water.
For example, he pumps water from a rusted water pump, but the water is so hot that it feels like two hundred degrees and tastes like battery acid.
He also sucks on stones to take his mind off thirst.
This shows how the setting features affect the cyclist’s physical and mental state.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the greatest obstacles was safety because most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, which is highly flammable.
Another obstacle was the constantly shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
Using lead weights to weigh down the back of the ship was neither practical nor safe because they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street.
The architects also had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the Empire State Building, which cost over sixty thousand dollars.
The building would now be 102 floors, with a glassed-in observation area on the 101st floor and an open observation platform on the 102nd floor.
This observation area was to double as the boarding area for dirigible passengers.
The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.
The final obtacle was the law.
There was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.
Two weeks later, another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
After this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.
In the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.

In the 1920s, dirigibles were considered to be the future of transportation.
Although useful, dirigibles had an issue, there was not enough landing area in New York City.
With this in mind, Al Smith saw an opportunity for his Empire State Building, he would construct a mooring mast on the top of the building.
This would allow dirigibles to anchor there for several hours, refuel, and also allow passengers go on and off.

Adding a mooring mast seemed full proof at the time but this new construction plan endured on many obstacles.The first obstacle was how to add a mooring mast without adding stress to the building's frame.
Architects detected that the stress of the dirigible's load and wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.
The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

The dirigibles could not be weighted down in the back with lead weights, as using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Two dirigibles attempted to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.

In February 1931, Irving Clavan of the building's architectural office said, "The as yet unsolved problems of mooring airships to a fixed mast at such a height made it desirable to postpone to a later date the final installation of the landing gear."

First, the architects had to design the mast.
They knew that the frame of the Empire state building would have to be strengthened to carry the load and wind pressure of the dirigible.

The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Although two dirigibles attempted to reach the building, they were unable to get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in their attempt to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Firstly, the building's frame could not support the stress of a thousand-foot dirigible moored at the top.
The steel frame had to be modified and strengthened to accommodate the new situation.
Secondly, the unpredictable wind atop the building made the idea of mooring a zeppelin very illogical.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
Thirdly, laws against flying low in urban areas were coming around.
These would make docking the airships to be illegal.
Safety was the biggest concern at each stage.
The recent explosion of the Hindenburg showed potential problems in docking these aircraft.
If a blimp was to explode in downtown New York, it could be a disaster.

Despite the challenges, the architects of the Empire State Building designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
However, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared by the late 1930s.
The unpredictable wind atop the building made the idea of mooring a zeppelin very illogical.
At this time, laws against flying low in urban areas were coming around.
These would make for docking the airships to be illegal.
The idea for making the Empire State Building a mooring post was an engineering feat but the actual usage of it was not practical.

Censorship is the practice of suppressing or removing materials that are considered obscene, politically unacceptable, or a threat to security.
This means that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., can be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, this practice is not fair to everyone and can limit the intellectual growth of individuals.
Firstly, censorship limits the freedom of people to access information.
If a book is removed from the library shelves because it is considered offensive, people who want to read it will not be able to do so.
This can be detrimental to the intellectual growth of individuals, as they will not be exposed to different ideas and perspectives.

For example, if a book about the Holocaust is removed from the library shelves because it is considered too graphic, people will not be able to learn about the atrocities that occurred during that time.
This can lead to a lack of understanding and empathy towards those who suffered during the Holocaust.
Secondly, censorship is subjective and can be biased.
What one person considers offensive, another person may find informative or enlightening.
For example, Katherine Paterson's quote highlights the fact that if one person has the right to remove a book they find offensive, then everyone else has the same right.
This means that books that are important for one person may be removed from the shelves because someone else finds them offensive.
This can limit the diversity of ideas and perspectives available in the library and hinder intellectual growth.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not fair to everyone and can limit the intellectual growth of individuals.
People should have the freedom to access information and ideas, even if they are considered offensive or controversial.
Censorship is subjective and can be biased, which means that people should be allowed to make their own decisions about what they want to read, watch, or listen to.
It is important for libraries to provide a diverse range of materials that cater to different interests and perspectives.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
The dirigibles were being hailed as the transportation of the future, but there was no suitable landing area in New York City.
The builders saw an opportunity to add a mooring mast to the top of the building to allow dirigibles to anchor there for several hours for refueling or service, and to let passengers off and on.
However, adding a mooring mast to the top of the building was not an easy task.
The builders had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the Empire State Building to accommodate the stress of the dirigible's load and wind pressure.
They also had to design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
However, the fate of the mooring mast was destined to never fulfill its purpose.
The greatest reason was one of safety: most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.
The greatest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.
Winds at the top of the building were shifting due to air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The architects also had to think about the existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
The builders didn't realize how complicated the process of even tying down a dirigible would be because of the high winds.
Even the process of dropping off newspapers was difficult, and took up too much time.

In "Winter Hibiscus" by Minfong Ho, Saeng, a Vietnamese immigrant, feels a sudden burst of recognition when she sees a hibiscus plant in a florist shop.
Memories of her childhood in Vietnam come flooding back to her, and she realizes how much she misses her home and family.
The story ends with Saeng vowing to retake her driver's test in the spring, after the geese return and the hibiscus is budding.
The author concludes the story this way to show that Saeng is still hopeful and optimistic, despite the challenges she faces as a newcomer to the United States.
She may feel homesick and out of place, but she is determined to succeed and make a new life for herself and her family.
By planting the hibiscus for her mother and vowing to retake the test, Saeng shows that she is willing to work hard and make sacrifices to achieve her goals.
Throughout the story, Saeng displays a strong connection to nature and the plants that remind her of home.
She is able to find comfort and solace in the familiar scents and textures of the flowers and leaves.
This connection to nature also reflects Saeng's resilience and ability to adapt to new environments.
Overall, "Winter Hibiscus" is a poignant and uplifting story about the immigrant experience and the power of hope and determination.
Saeng's story shows that even in the face of adversity, we can find strength and comfort in the things that remind us of home.
Saeng finished digging the hole for the new flower for her mother, so her mom could go make dinner.
As she stood up, she felt a sense of determination wash over her.
She was going to retake that driver's test and pass it, no matter how scared she was.
The hibiscus plant reminded her of her home and her family, and it gave her the strength to keep going.
Saeng's story is a reminder that even when we feel lost and alone, there is always hope.
She may be a newcomer to the United States, but she is determined to make a new life for herself and her family.
She knows that it won't be easy, but she is willing to work hard and make sacrifices to achieve her goals.
Throughout the story, Saeng shows us the power of nature and the importance of finding comfort in the familiar.
She may be far from home, but the plants and flowers around her remind her of where she came from and give her the strength to keep going.
Saeng's story is a testament to the resilience of the human spirit and the power of hope.
In the end, Saeng's vow to retake her driver's test in the spring is a symbol of her determination and her refusal to give up.
She knows that it won't be easy, but she is willing to try again.
She was scared, but through everything Saeng had hope, a positive attitude, and she was helpful.

No, a better piece of advice for the solo cyclist would be, “Never accept travel advice from a collection of old-timers who haven’t left the confines of their porches since Carter was in office.” It’s not that a group of old guys doesn’t know the terrain.
With age comes wisdom and all that, but the world is a fluid place.

He hardly noticed the “sun was beginning to beat down.” He was calm and was looking forward to the “cool pines and rushing rivers of Yosemite.” Never once did he imagine what he had gotten himself into.
As he began to approach the desert, he noticed he was running low on water.
The strenuous activity of biking combine d with the scorching heat of the desert began to take effect.
The cyclist was so desperate for water that he had to put pebbles into his mouth.
He had once read, “that sucking on stones helps take your mind off thirst by allowing what spit you have left to circulate.” The cyclist was hoping for a way out of the misery he had come across.
Dehydration took it’s toll, and he felt hallucinations.
He was beginning to lose hope.
The heat and the hills and the lack of water had the greatest affect on the cyclist.
At a reservoir campground outside of Lodi, California, the cyclist had received some travel advice from a group of old-timers.
The old guys had pointed out landmarks and spouted off towns that the cyclist would come across on his ride to Yosemite National Park.
The cyclist had followed their advice and launched out at first light along a “shortcut” that was to slice away hours from his ride.
The old guys had sworn that the next town was only eighteen miles down the road.
The cyclist had believed them, but things began to change.
Flat road was replaced by short, rolling hills.
The speed limit was 55 mph, and the cyclist was doing a water-depleting 12 mph.
The terrain was changing, and the cyclist was running low on water.
He had been hitting his water bottles pretty regularly, but he was traveling through the high deserts of California in June.
The cyclist was hoping to make it to the next town, but he arrived at a ghost town instead.
The town was deserted and the water from the rusted pump was brackish and tasted like battery acid.
The cyclist began to break the ride down into distances he could see on the horizon, telling himself that if he could make it that far, he’d be fine.

She could have easily lost her patience and gotten angry, but she didn't.
Instead, she remained calm and continued to wait.
She even called the company a few times to ask about the package, but she never raised her voice or got angry.

My mom was so happy and excited that she didn't even care that it had taken so long to arrive.
She opened the package and found that everything was in perfect condition.
She was thrilled that she had been patient and had waited for it to arrive.
My mom's patience taught me a valuable lesson.
I learned that it's important to stay calm and patient even when things don't go as planned.

If you can remain patient, you'll be able to handle any situation that comes your way.
But the whole time stayed calm and patient.

As Katherine Paterson, author of Bridge to Terabithia, said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This quote perfectly sums up my stance on censorship.
Censorship violates our right to freedom of expression and our right to access information.
It is not up to a few individuals to decide what is appropriate for everyone else to read or watch.
Just because someone finds a book or movie offensive does not mean that it should be removed from the shelves.
Furthermore, censorship limits our exposure to diverse perspectives and ideas.
We live in a world filled with different cultures, beliefs, and opinions.
By censoring certain materials, we are depriving ourselves of the opportunity to learn about different perspectives and ideas that may challenge our own beliefs.
Lastly, let's say that in a library, theres at least one book to each person in a community that offends that person.
If they were each given the right to remove the book that offended them, what would be left to read?
And each of those people that removed a book, most likely would enjoy another book that someone thought was offensive.
So now there isn't a single book for that person to read, just because everyone else disliked the books they didn't think were offensive.
Once someone starts removing, other people will join in, and you'd be left with an empty library.
Thats what I think about cencorship.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the answer to protecting our children or ourselves from offensive materials.
Instead, we should embrace the diversity of perspectives and ideas that exist in our world.
We should encourage open-mindedness and critical thinking rather than censorship.

I believe that people should have the right to read what they want, without any censorship.
Firstly, censorship can limit our access to important information.

For example, books about history or politics may contain information that some people find offensive, but it is important for us to learn about these topics in order to understand the world around us.
By removing these books from libraries, we are limiting our ability to learn and grow as individuals.
What one person finds offensive, another may not.
Therefore, it is not fair to limit everyone's access to certain materials based on one person's opinion.
This is why I believe that it should be up to the individual reader to decide whether or not they want to read a particular book or watch a particular movie.
Lastly, censorship can lead to a slippery slope.
If we start removing books or other materials that are deemed offensive, where do we draw the line?
Who decides what is offensive and what is not?
Allowing censorship can lead to a situation where nothing is allowed, and we are left with an empty library.
In conclusion, I firmly believe that people should have the right to read what they want, without any censorship.
Censorship limits our access to important information, can be subjective, and can lead to a slippery slope.
As Katherine Paterson once said, "And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us".
All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.

In the story "Winter Hibiscus" by Minfong Ho, Saeng moves to the United States from Vietnam and struggles to adjust to her new home.
She feels homesick and disconnected from her culture and memories of her grandmother.
However, when Saeng sees a hibiscus plant at a florist shop, it reminds her of her childhood in Vietnam and brings back memories of her grandmother's hair and the well with red blossoms.
She buys the plant, but it is not the same as the saebba hedge she had in Vietnam.
Saeng is disappointed and feels a wave of loss, but her mother helps her plant the "winter hibiscus" in their garden.
The author concludes the story with Saeng vowing to retake her driver's test in the spring when the geese return and the hibiscus is budding.
This ending conveys persistence and renewal.
Like the winter hibiscus, Saeng is hardy and can come back from disappointment and failure.
The plant doesn't die each season and is beautiful and indomitable, just like Saeng wants to be.
She sees the plant as a symbol of her ability to renew herself and keep going, even in a new and unfamiliar place.
Saeng's determination to retake the test shows that she is willing to work hard and not give up, just like the winter hibiscus.
She vowed to herself that when the day comes again she will be ready to renew herself and get back on track.
The plant doesn’t die each season.
If the girl can be persistant and come back next year to retake the test, she will be considered persistant.
Furthermore, the "winter hibiscus" also represents the idea of adaptation.
Saeng realizes that the hibiscus may not be the same as the saebba hedge she had in Vietnam, but it is still beautiful and can survive in the harsh winter climate of the United States.
Similarly, Saeng must adapt to her new surroundings and find beauty and strength in her new life.
No matter where the plant is being grown, it will always keep those traits.

Additionally, nature itself was an obstacle, as winds at the top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
These challenges made it difficult for the builders to create a practical and safe way to dock dirigibles at the building.
Ultimately, the idea was abandoned due to safety concerns and the rise of airplane travel.
The rooms that were set aside for dirigible passengers were repurposed into a soda fountain and tea garden for sightseers.
Overall, the builders faced significant challenges in attempting to make the Empire State Building a destination for dirigibles.

She goes to a florist shop to see if the plant can be purchased and is overwhelmed by the greenery she sees.

She purchases the hibiscus plant and takes it home to her mother.
Her mother is surprised but happy to see the plant.
Saeng then promises herself that she will retake her driver's test in the spring, once the hibiscus plant has budded.
The author concludes the story with Saeng's promise because it shows that she has found something to motivate herself.
The hibiscus plant has become a symbol of hope and familiarity for Saeng.
She is determined to retake her driver's test and succeed.
The hibiscus plant has given her the strength to keep going and not give up.
In conclusion, Saeng's purchase of the hibiscus plant represents her longing for familiarity in a new and unfamiliar environment.
The plant helps her to remember her past and gives her the motivation to keep moving forward.
Saeng's promise to retake her driver's test in the spring shows that she is not giving up and is determined to succeed.
The author decided to end the story with this promise to highlight Saeng's resilience and determination.
She then proceeded to purchase the plant, because she failed the test she needed something to lift her spirits back up once again.

Everyone has different opinions and beliefs, and just because someone doesn't like a certain book doesn't mean that others won't enjoy it.
Furthermore, censorship limits our freedom of speech and expression.
We should be able to read, watch, and listen to whatever we want without fear of censorship.
It is important to have access to different viewpoints and opinions, even if we don't necessarily agree with them.
By censoring materials, we are limiting our own knowledge and understanding of the world.

Children should be exposed to different ideas and perspectives, and by censoring materials, we are limiting their learning opportunities.
Children should be able to explore different topics and ideas without fear of censorship.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the solution.

As a society, we should be able to access different viewpoints and perspectives, even if we don't necessarily agree with them.

Architects of the Empire State Building faced a tremendous amount of obstacles when they attempted to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Al Smith, the man who wanted to construct the tallest building, stated on December 11, 1929, that the Empire State would be 1,250 feet tall.
It was decided that the building would have a mooring mast at the top for docking airships like the dirigibles.
The blimps, however, was very spacey.
Some were as long as one thousand feet in length.
So a mooring mast sounds fitting.
It would allow dirigibles/blimps to anchor there to refuel as well as letting the passengers off and on.Presently, the purpose of the mooring mast was never carried out.
Problems that faced it was that most dirigibles outside of the United States used hydrogen instead of helium.

Hydrogen is highly flammable and the German dirigible Hindenburg incident caused the Empire S Building's owners to realize how bad it would be if it happened above such a densely populated area like New York.
The winds on top of the building is always changing.
A dirigible tethered to the mooring mast would have the back of the ship swivel around and around.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
In conclusion, the Empire State Building faced many obstacles when designing the mooring mast to dock airships like dirigibles.
The biggest obstacle was the safety factor concerning the use of hydrogen as a fuel source for dirigibles.
The other obstacles were the constant changing winds on top of the building and the law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
All of these factors contributed to the ultimate decision to abandon the idea of docking dirigibles at the Empire State Building.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the greatest obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
If an accident were to occur above a densely populated area like downtown New York, it could be catastrophic.
Another obstacle was the constantly shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

The back of the ship could be weighted down with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
There was also an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, which made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Finally, the dirigible industry was giving way to airplanes, and the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.
But with this came lots of work.
And they couldn't simply drop a mooring mast on top of the building.
They had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the building to accommodate the new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.
The architects designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
The building would now be 102 floors, with a glassed-in observation area on the 101st floor and an open observation platform on the 102nd floor.
This observation area was to double as the boarding area for dirigible passengers.
When the building had been framed to the 85th floor, the roof had to be completed before the framing for the mooring mast could take place.
The mast also had a skeleton of steel and was clad in stainless steel with glass windows."

Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
If an accident were to happen above downtown New York, it could be catastrophic.
The violent winds on top of the building were also a problem.
Even if a dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Without the dirigible being held down, the violent winds would push the ship into sharp spires that would rip the shell.
With the wind pressure and the dirigible's load itself, there would be too much stress being added to the building's frame.
The building's steel frame required over sixty thousand dollars in modifications to transmit the stress nearly eleven hundred feet down to the foundation.
The existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas was another obstacle.

As a student and a frequent visitor to my local library, I strongly believe that censorship in libraries should not be enforced.
Censorship is defined as the suppression or prohibition of any parts of books, films, news, etc.
that are considered obscene, politically unacceptable, or a threat to security.
However, I believe that censorship is not the solution to eliminating the problem of offensive materials in libraries.
Firstly, censorship goes against the First Amendment of the United States Constitution, which guarantees freedom of speech and expression for all citizens.
By censoring materials in libraries, we are limiting the freedom of expression of authors and artists who create these materials.
Everyone has the right to express themselves and share their ideas with others, even if some may find it offensive.
It is up to the individual to decide whether or not they want to engage with that material.
Secondly, censorship is subjective and can vary from person to person.
What one person might find offensive, another might find valuable and informative.
By censoring materials, we are limiting the opportunity for individuals to learn and gain knowledge about different perspectives and ideas.
It is important to have a diverse range of materials available in libraries to cater to the interests and needs of all individuals.
Moreover, censorship does not solve the problem of offensive materials in libraries.
It simply hides the problem and does not address the root cause of why these materials are considered offensive in the first place.
It is important to have open and honest discussions about these materials and why they may be considered offensive.
This allows individuals to understand different perspectives and develop their own opinions about the materials.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries should not be enforced.
It goes against the First Amendment, limits the opportunity for individuals to learn and gain knowledge, and does not solve the problem of offensive materials in libraries.
Instead, we should focus on having open and honest discussions about these materials and why they may be considered offensive.

In the essay "Rough Road Ahead" by Joe Kurmaskie, the features of the setting have a significant impact on the cyclist.
The harsh and unforgiving terrain, scorching heat, and lack of water make the journey to Yosemite National Park a daunting one.
The cyclist's decision to listen to the advice of a group of old-timers who have not left their porches in years proves to be a grave mistake.
The cyclist's troubles begin when he takes a shortcut suggested by the old men.
The route is desolate and barren, and the cyclist struggles to find water.
The old water pump he comes across does not work, and the water tastes like battery acid.
The cyclist is forced to ration his water and go inward to conserve his energy.
The terrain becomes even more challenging as the cyclist encounters rolling hills and tumbleweeds.
The heat is oppressive, and the cyclist is dehydrated and exhausted.
He comes across an abandoned Welch's Grape Juice factory, which only adds to his despair.
Finally, the cyclist stumbles upon Gary and Wilber's Fish Camp, where he is able to quench his thirst and rest.
The old man he meets there tells him the best way to get to Yosemite and offers him directions.
However, the cyclist has learned his lesson and decides to rely on his map instead.
In conclusion, the setting of the essay has a significant impact on the cyclist.
The harsh terrain, extreme heat, and lack of water all contribute to the cyclist's struggle.
The cyclist's decision to listen to the advice of the old-timers and his lack of preparation for the climate nearly cost him his life.
However, he learns from his mistakes and decides to rely on his map in the future.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Most dirigibles used gas instead of helium, which is highly flammable.
If a dirigible caught fire, it could cause a lot of damage and kill many pedestrians in the densely populated area below.
Additionally, dirigibles were difficult to control, and the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Finally, there was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, making it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
The dirigibles used gas instead of helium, so it was very flammable.

The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
The building would now be 102 floors, with a glassed-in observation area on the 101st floor and an open observation platform on the 102nd floor.

He describes his childhood home in the Ironbound section of Newark, New Jersey, as a simple house where his parents created a traditional Cuban home.
The heart of the home was the kitchen, where his parents shared cooking duties and instilled in him a love of cooking.
The innocence of childhood, the congregation of family and friends, and endless celebrations formed the backdrop to life in their warm home.

Despite living in a neighborhood made up of mostly Spanish, Cuban, and Italian immigrants at a time when overt racism was the norm, Rodriguez's parents kept their arms and their door open to people who were clearly in need.

Rodriguez is grateful to his parents for their love and sacrifice, and he will never forget the lessons they taught him about the importance of family and friends.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Firstly, the stress of a thousand-foot dirigible held by a single cable tether would add stress to the building's frame.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars' worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
Secondly, the winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
Thirdly, most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Another reason why it was unsafe because if some of the glass or steel part got pushed off the people down be low.
Furthermore, the law against airships flying too low over urban areas would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped, they both faced challenges.
The U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

The captain could not even take his hands off the control levers for fear that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell.
Two weeks later, another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
Because the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, a worker atop the mooring mast would have to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt, the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.

In conclusion, the builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there, including the stress on the building's frame, shifting winds, flammability of hydrogen, safety concerns, and legal restrictions.

In the story "Winter Hibiscus" by Minfong Ho, Saeng moves to the United States from Vietnam with her family.
She fails her driver’s test and feels disappointed because her mother is disappointed in her.
However, when she sees the hibiscus plant, it reminds her of her childhood in Vietnam.
She feels nostalgic and remembers her grandmother, the saebba hedge, and the dok Malik.
She feels a deep sense of loss and weeps.
Later, when she plants the winter hibiscus, she thinks about the geese flying in the sky and decides to take the test again in the spring.

The author concludes the story with the sentence, "When they come back, Saeng vowed silently to herself, in the spring, when the snows melt and the geese return and this hibiscus is budding, then I will take that test again."
This is because Saeng is determined to pass the test and believes she can do it.
She feels a sense of hope and renewal as she looks forward to the future.
She knows she can do it and is ready to take on the challenge.
She feels disapointed because her mom is disapointed in her and knows she can pass it.
Saeng's determination is evident throughout the story.
She is determined to find the hibiscus plant, even when the florist doesn't understand what she is looking for.
She is determined to buy the plant, even though it is expensive.
She is determined to plant it, even though the soil is hard and cold.
And now, she is determined to pass her driver's test.
Saeng's determination is also a reflection of her resilience.
She has moved to a new country, learned a new language, and adapted to a new culture.
She has faced disappointment and loss, but she has also found comfort in familiar things like the hibiscus plant and the dok Malik.
She has learned to appreciate the beauty of bitter melon and the sound of Canada geese.
Now that she is determined to take the test, she is going to take it at the same time in the next year and she believes she is going to pass it.
In the short story "Winter Hibiscus" by Minfong Ho, the author concludes the story with Saeng vowing to retake her driver's test in the spring.
This ending shows Saeng's growth and maturity.
Throughout the story, Saeng struggles with her identity and homesickness after moving to the United States from Vietnam.
She finds comfort in the familiar plants she sees at a florist shop and buys a "winter hibiscus" to plant in her garden.
However, her failure to pass her driver's test adds to her feelings of inadequacy and displacement.
The ending of the story shows Saeng's determination to succeed and make her parents proud.
By vowing to retake her driver's test in the spring, Saeng is showing her willingness to learn and grow.
She no longer wants to disappoint her parents and wants to prove to them that she can adapt to life in the United States.
This shows her maturity and willingness to take responsibility for her actions.
Overall, the ending of "Winter Hibiscus" is a hopeful one.
It shows that Saeng is finding her place in her new home and is willing to work hard to succeed.

One time, my family and I went on a camping trip.
We set up our tent near a lake and spent the day swimming and fishing.
That night, we decided to make a campfire and roast some marshmallows.
We told each other scary stories and laughed at how scared we were.
As the night went on, we started to hear strange noises coming from the woods.
We all got a little bit scared and started to joke around about it.
My dad pretended to be a bear and chased us around the campfire.
We were all laughing so hard that we forgot about being scared.
Suddenly, my little brother got up to go to the bathroom.
He walked a few feet away from the campfire and then we heard a loud splash.
We all got really quiet and then heard him yell “I fell in the lake!”  We all ran over to him and saw that he was soaking wet.
We asked him what happened and he said that he had tripped over a rock and fallen into the lake.
We all started laughing at him and he started to laugh too.
We helped him dry off and then went back to the campfire.
For the rest of the night, we made jokes about my brother falling in the lake.
Every time someone said something funny, we all laughed so hard that our stomachs hurt.
We stayed up late into the night, telling jokes and making each other laugh.
That camping trip was one of the best times that my family and I had together.
We bonded over our shared laughter and made memories that we will never forget.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the biggest obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside the United States used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
Another obstacle was the shifting winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Additionally, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
Finally, the builders also faced a major obstacle of money.
They wanted to redo the framework, which cost over sixty thousand dollars.
It must've and hard working that high up dealing with some rain, fog, and mostly, the wind.

The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.

In conclusion, the builders faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock at the Empire State Building, including safety concerns, shifting winds, an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas, and the cost of modifying the building's framework.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles while attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
All the builders had to start off by making a mooring mast at the top of the building.
They had to modify and strengthen the steel frame of the building to accommodate the dirigible's load and wind pressure.
Over sixty thousand dollars worth of modifications had to be made to the building's framework.
They designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
However, the dirigible mast was doomed to fail because of safety concerns.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable, and an accident like the Hindenburg disaster could have catastrophic effects on a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible was tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas also made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

In the essay “Rough Road Ahead” by Joe Kurmaskie, the setting has a significant impact on the solo cyclist.
The cyclist is traveling from a reservoir campground outside of Lodi, California, to Yosemite National Park.
He encounters a group of old-timers who give him advice on a shortcut.
However, the journey turns out to be much more difficult than he anticipated.
The first challenge the cyclist faces is the lack of water.
He pumps water from a rusty pump, but it is too hot and tastes like battery acid.
He conserves his water and tries to push through to the next town, but it is further away than the old-timers had claimed.
The terrain becomes hilly, and the cyclist struggles to maintain his speed.
He encounters a sign warning of a rough road ahead, and he realizes he is in trouble.
The cyclist faces physical exhaustion and dehydration due to the setting.
He is in a high desert area in June, and the heat is unbearable.
He is forced to suck on stones to help alleviate his thirst.
He becomes delirious and starts to lose hope, thinking he might not survive.
However, he manages to push through and finally reaches Gary and Wilber’s Fish Camp, where he can drink from a sink and recover.
In conclusion, the setting has a significant impact on the cyclist in “Rough Road Ahead.” The lack of water, hilly terrain, and extreme heat all contribute to his physical exhaustion and dehydration.
He is forced to push through his limits to survive.
Then he said “over the long crippling hill, a building came into view.” It is at this point that he uses the word “crippling” because he is just about exhausted and can’t go any further.
There are several features of the setting that affect the cyclist in many ways.
For example, the setting of one ramshackle shed, rusty pumps, and a corral affected the cyclist.
This setting troubled the cyclist, as stated in the essay.
When the cyclist came to this kind of setting, it threw him off course a little.
The cyclist probably wasn't expecting to run into some old, ragged place where he couldn't even pump water, and when he did the water didn't taste as normal, clean water does.
This probably slowed him down also, considering he needed water.
Another setting feature that affected the cyclist was when he encounters a snake, a large one at that, and some tumbleweeds.
This setting made the cyclist feel scared and unsure of what was going to happen next.
He was already low on water and this didn't help his situation.
Moreover, the setting of the "Rough Road Ahead" sign affected the cyclist in a negative way.
This setting made the cyclist feel hopeless and miserable.
The sign indicated that the road ahead would be a challenge, and the cyclist was already struggling with dehydration.
The cyclist was only doing 12 mph and the sign indicated a speed limit of 55 mph.
This meant that the cyclist was going to be on the road for a long time.
Lastly, the setting of approaching the bait shop affected him.
This feature gave the cyclist hope and relief because he was finally around something and had a decent water supply.
In conclusion many if not all of the settings the cyclist encounters affects him in a way.

There were many obstacles the builders of the Empire State Building faced in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One example is that by adding the dirigible, it would add stress to the building.
The stress of the dirigible’s load and the wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building’s foundation, which was nearly eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the Empire State Building would have to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation.
Over sixty thousand dollars’ worth of modifications had to be made to the building’s framework.

The architects had designed a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.

The winches and control machinery for the dirigible mooring would be housed in the base of the shaft itself, which also housed elevators and stairs to bring passengers down to the eighty-sixth floor, where baggage and ticket areas would be located.
Now, there would also be 102 floors.
The top floor would be the boarding area as well as an observation area.
One more thing they had done for the mooring masts was raise an American flag on top.
However, the biggest obstacle was safety.
Most of the dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen which was highly flammable.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.
This made it dangerous for pedestrians on the street below.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.

She breaks down and weeps in the warm, moist shelter of the greenhouse.
Saeng's mother notices the tearstains on her daughter's cheeks and her puffy eyes and asks her what happened.
Saeng tells her that she failed her driver's test.
Her mother comforts her and tells her that the winter hibiscus is strong enough to make it through the cold months here.
Saeng vows to herself that she will take the test again in the spring when the geese return and the hibiscus is budding.
The author concludes the story with Saeng's vow because it shows that Saeng is adapting to her new life in the United States.
Saeng has found comfort in the familiar plants and scents from her childhood in Vietnam.
She is determined to take the test again and pass it, showing that she is willing to work hard and adapt to her new environment.

Censorship is a topic that has been debated for many years.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
Others believe that censorship is wrong and that people should have the freedom to read, watch, or listen to whatever they want.
In my opinion, I believe that certain materials should not be banned from libraries.
As Katherine Paterson said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This means that if we start banning books or other materials, then eventually there will be nothing left for anyone to read or watch.
Instead of banning offensive materials, we should allow people to make their own decisions.
If they believe the material is too mature for their child, they could restrict them.
If the item doesn't seem too harmful, they could allow it.
That decision, however, is up to the parents.
Books or movies that are considered offensive could also be given their own section of a library.
Children would not be allowed in that section without parental supervision.
And that, again, is the decision of the child's parents.
There are many reasons why offensive material should not be banned.
That sort of material, however, should have restrictions on who should and should not check them out.
