The builders of the Empire State Building face various obstacles in their attempts to make a statement by constructing the world's tallest building.
They were determined to outstrip the seventy-seven-story Chrysler Building in height, which was then the tallest building before the Empire State began construction.
However, the architect building the Chrysler Building had a trick up his sleeve.

He secretly constructed a 185-foot spire inside the building and hoisted it up to the top of the Chrysler Building, bringing it to a height of 1,046 feet, 46 feet taller than the originally announced height of the Empire State Building.
This challenged the Empire State Building's builders to rush to lay out new plans to win the title of world's tallest building.
Furthermore, the master that was to be attached to the Empire State proved to have designing issues.
The mast was not just an ornament, but it served a higher calling, that is, to accommodate the passengers of the new airships, which were then only the dream of aviation pioneers.

The architects had to design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower that would be illuminated from inside, with a stepped-back design that imitated the overall shape of the building itself.
The rocket-shaped mast would have four wings at its corners, of shiny aluminum, and would rise to a conical roof that would house the mooring arm.
However, the biggest obstacle to the successful use of the mooring mast was nature itself.

The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents, and even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other practical reason why dirigibles could not moor at the Empire State Building was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.
In addition, most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.

Therefore, the mooring mast of the Empire State Building was destined to never fulfill its purpose, and the rooms that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world’s highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.

The excerpt "The Mooring Mast" by Marcia Amidon Lüted explains the construction of the Empire State Building in New York.
The excerpt explains the steps of building the building as well is the obstacles and challenges that the builder faced.

The architects of building the Empire State Building attempted to allow dirigibles to dock there, did not take into account the problems that may come with taking on such a large project.The creator of this plan to build a docking mast on the Empire State Building was Al Smith.
The creator of this plan to build a docking mast on the Empire State Building was Al Smith.
One of the obstacles that the builders faced was the stress that a thousand-foot dirigible would add to the building's frame.
The dirigible's load and wind pressure would have to be transmitted all the way to the building's foundation, almost eleven hundred feet below.
The steel frame of the building had to be modified and strengthened to accommodate this new situation, which cost over sixty thousand dollars.
Another obstacle was the constant shifting of winds on top of the building due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
The other obstacle was an existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible's shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
By the late 1930s, the idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared.

The rooms in the Empire State Building that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world's highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.
The highest open observation deck, intended for disembarking passengers, has never been open to the public.

This essay is all about wether certain materials in libraries should be removed from the shelves if they are offensive to some.
I do not believe things should be removed from shelves in libraries if they offened someone.
Firstly, everyone has different opinions and beliefs.
What might be offensive to one person, might not be offensive to another.
Removing books or other materials from the shelves just because someone finds them offensive is not fair to everyone else who might enjoy them.
We should not be censoring what others can read, watch, or listen to just because some people don't like it.
Secondly, censorship can limit our knowledge and understanding of the world.
If we only read or watch things that we agree with or that are deemed "appropriate", then we are not challenging ourselves or expanding our perspectives.
We might miss out on important information or different viewpoints that could help us grow as individuals.
Lastly, censorship goes against our right to freedom of speech and expression.
We should all have the right to read, watch, or listen to whatever we want without fear of it being taken away.
If we start censoring materials in libraries, where does it stop?
Who decides what is offensive and what is not?
We could end up with a society where only certain ideas and beliefs are allowed, and that is not a society that values diversity and individuality.
In conclusion, I believe that books, music, movies, magazines, and other materials should not be removed from library shelves just because they offend some people.
We should be able to make our own choices about what we want to read, watch, or listen to without fear of censorship.
As Katherine Paterson said, "we have no books left on the shelf for any of us" if we start removing things just because some people don't like them.
Censorship in libraries is a topic that has been debated for years.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I believe that censorship in libraries is not a good idea.
Katherine Paterson, an author, once said, "'All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us'."
This quote perfectly sums up my opinion on censorship in libraries.
If we start removing books that some people find offensive, then soon there will be no books left on the shelves for anyone to read.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced several obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
Most dirigibles used hydrogen, which is highly flammable.
The Hindenburg disaster in 1937 made it clear that allowing dirigibles to dock above a densely populated area like downtown New York was too dangerous.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Also, a dirigible had to be weighted down or it'd spin around the mast and the commonly used lead weights were a hazard for pedestrians below.
Another obstacle was the existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas.
This law would make it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area, although two dirigibles did attempt to reach the building before the entire idea was dropped.
In December 1930, the U.S. Navy dirigible Los Angeles approached the mooring mast but could not get close enough to tie up because of forceful winds.

Fearing that the wind would blow the dirigible onto the sharp spires of other buildings in the area, which would puncture the dirigible’s shell, the captain could not even take his hands off the control levers.
Two weeks later, another dirigible, the Goodyear blimp Columbia, attempted a publicity stunt where it would tie up and deliver a bundle of newspapers to the Empire State Building.
Because the complete dirigible mooring equipment had never been installed, a worker atop the mooring mast would have to catch the bundle of papers on a rope dangling from the blimp.
The papers were delivered in this fashion, but after this stunt the idea of using the mooring mast was shelved.
Design, safety, and legal issues all were obstacles which got the better of the builders.

The builders of the Empire State Building faced many obstacles in attempting to allow dirigibles to dock there.
One of the obstacles was safety.
Most dirigibles from outside of the United States used hydrogen rather than helium, and hydrogen is highly flammable.

When the German dirigible Hindenburg was destroyed by fire in Lakehurst, New Jersey, on May 6, 1937, the owners of the Empire State Building realized how much worse that accident could have been if it had taken place above a densely populated area such as downtown New York.
The winds on top of the building were constantly shifting due to violent air currents.
Even if the dirigible were tethered to the mooring mast, the back of the ship would swivel around and around the mooring mast.

Dirigibles moored in open landing fields could be weighted down in the back with lead weights, but using these at the Empire State Building, where they would be dangling high above pedestrians on the street, was neither practical nor safe.
Lastly, there was the reason of the law.
An existing law against airships flying too low over urban areas made it illegal for a ship to ever tie up to the building or even approach the area.

Despite the architects' efforts to modify and strengthen the building's framework and design a shiny glass and chrome-nickel stainless steel tower with a rocket-shaped mast, the mooring mast of the Empire State Building was destined to never fulfill its purpose.
The idea of using the mooring mast for dirigibles and their passengers had quietly disappeared by the late 1930s.

The rooms that had been set aside for the ticketing and baggage of dirigible passengers were made over into the world's highest soda fountain and tea garden for use by the sightseers who flocked to the observation decks.
The highest open observation deck, intended for disembarking passengers, has never been open to the public.
They could've taken risks on the other theories, but on this one they had no choice.
They wouldn't be able to fight the law to allow dirigibles to fly that low.
To conclude, the obstacles faced by the builders of safety, nature, and law could not be overcome to get the mast up and working.

As a student, I strongly believe that censorship in libraries is a complex issue that requires careful consideration.
While some materials may be offensive to certain individuals or groups, it is not fair to remove them from the shelves altogether.

As Katherine Paterson, author of many famous books, has said, "if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
In my opinion, censorship limits our freedom of speech and access to information.
It is important to remember that what is considered offensive varies from person to person.
For example, some people may find books that contain LGBTQ+ characters offensive, while others may find books that include religious themes offensive.
If we start removing all materials that someone finds offensive, there will be nothing left on the shelves for anyone to read.
However, I do believe that libraries have a responsibility to provide appropriate materials for different age groups.
Some books, movies, and music may not be suitable for children, and it is important to have a system of ratings and warnings to help parents make informed decisions.
This way, libraries can still provide a wide variety of materials without compromising the well-being of young readers.
Moreover, censorship can be harmful to the community.
By removing certain materials, we are limiting the opportunity for individuals to learn about different perspectives and experiences.
We need to be exposed to different ideas, even if they are not always agreeable to us.
This is how we grow and learn as individuals.

Censorship in libraries is a topic that has been debated for many years.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I believe that censorship in libraries is not the answer.
In fact, it can do more harm than good.
Firstly, censorship limits our freedom of expression.
As stated by Katherine Paterson, if we have the right to remove a book from the shelf, then everyone else has the same right.
This means that if one person finds a book offensive, they have the power to remove it from the library.
This is not fair to those who may want to read the book and form their own opinions.
Everyone has the right to read what they want, and censorship takes that right away.
Secondly, censorship can lead to ignorance.
By removing certain materials from the library, we are preventing people from learning about different cultures and perspectives.
For example, if a book talks about a certain religion, and someone finds it offensive, they may want to remove it from the shelf.
However, by doing so, they are preventing others from learning about that religion and forming their own opinions.
Censorship can limit our knowledge and understanding of the world around us.
What one person finds offensive, another person may not.
For example, if someone finds a book with sexual content offensive, they may want it removed from the library.
However, someone else may find the book informative and helpful.
Censorship can lead to a never-ending cycle of removing materials from the library based on personal opinions, which can be unfair and ultimately limit our knowledge and understanding of the world.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not the answer.
It limits our freedom of expression, can lead to ignorance, and can be subjective.
Instead, we should focus on educating ourselves and others about different cultures and perspectives.
We should also respect each other's opinions and allow everyone to have the right to read what they want.
Censorship is not the solution, and we should strive to create an environment where everyone feels comfortable learning and growing.

Patience is an important virtue that we all need to have.
It means being understanding and tolerant.
One time, my friend Janine showed great patience when we were waiting for our food at a restaurant.
We were really hungry and the food was taking a long time to arrive.
I was getting frustrated and wanted to leave, but Janine stayed calm and said that we should wait a little longer.
She reminded me that the restaurant was probably very busy and that the cooks were doing their best to prepare our food.
We waited for about 20 more minutes before our food finally arrived.
It was delicious and we were glad that we stayed.
Another example of patience is when my dad and I went deer hunting.
We had to wait for hours in the woods without making any noise.
You have to be patient to wait for deer.
They don't always come sometimes it could just be a fawn.
We sat there for hours, listening to the sounds of the forest and waiting for the perfect moment to take a shot.
My dad told me that patience was the key to being a good hunter.
You couldn't rush things or you would scare away the deer.
We waited and waited until finally, we saw a buck in the distance.
We didn't move or make any noise.
It took a long time, but eventually, the buck started to move closer to us.
We stayed still and waited for the perfect moment to take a shot.
When it finally came, we were ready.
My dad took the shot and the buck went down.
Being patient is not always easy, but it is an important skill to have.
Whether you are waiting for food at a restaurant or waiting for a deer to come into range, patience is key.
You have to be willing to wait and be understanding of the situation.
If you rush things, you may miss out on something important.
So, the next time you find yourself getting impatient, take a deep breath and remember that good things come to those who wait.

He encountered tumbleweeds and a large snake, which made him lose his balance.
He was running low on water and was desperate to find a water source.
He stumbled upon an abandoned Welch’s Grape Juice factory and bottling plant, which added to his misery.
The setting affected the cyclist's physical and mental state.
He was dehydrated, fatigued and had lost all hope of surviving.
He had to suck on stones to quench his thirst and take his mind off it.
The setting also affected his decision-making skills as he listened to the wrong advice from the old men.
He learned his lesson and promised himself to stick to his map in the future.

It affected his physical and mental state and his decision-making skills.
The cyclist learned to be more cautious and to rely on his map instead of taking advice from strangers.

On the other hand, others argue that censorship is a violation of the First Amendment and that people should have the right to access any material they choose.

Furthermore, I believe that censorship can be a slippery slope.
If we start removing books or other materials that some find offensive, where do we draw the line?
Who gets to decide what is offensive and what is not?

Going to the library you would think of it as an family environment, wouldn't you?
It's a place where you can find books, movies, and music for everyone, from children to adults.
But what happens when some people find certain materials, such as books, offensive?
Should they have the right to remove them from the shelves?
In my opinion, censorship in libraries is not a good idea.
Everyone has different opinions and beliefs, and what one person finds offensive, another person might find enlightening or even life-changing.
If we start removing books, music, and movies that some people find offensive, where do we draw the line?
Who gets to decide what's offensive and what's not?
Katherine Paterson, author of many beloved children's books, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.
But if I have the right to remove that book from the shelf -- that work I abhor -- then you also have exactly the same right and so does everyone else.
And then we have no books left on the shelf for any of us."
This is a very important point.
If we start removing books that some people find offensive, we might end up removing all the books from the shelves.
Furthermore, censorship can limit our freedom of speech and expression.
If we start censoring books, music, and movies, we might start censoring other things as well, like art or political speech.
This is not what our country stands for.
We should be able to express ourselves freely, even if some people don't agree with us.
Of course, there are some materials that should not be available in libraries, like pornography or hate speech.
Most books, music, and movies are not harmful, even if some people find them offensive.
We should trust our fellow citizens to make their own decisions about what they want to read, watch, or listen to.
In conclusion, censorship in libraries is not a good idea.
It limits our freedom of speech and expression and can lead to a slippery slope where we start censoring everything.
We should trust people to make their own decisions about what they want to read, watch, or listen to, even if we don't agree with them.

In the essay "Rough Road Ahead" by Joe Kurmaskie, the features of the setting have a significant impact on the cyclist.
Throughout his journey to Yosemite, the cyclist faces various challenges that affect him both mentally and physically.
The deserted town, lack of water, hot weather, and abandoned factory create a feeling of desperation in the cyclist.
He is forced to suck on stones to help alleviate his thirst, and he begins to fear that he may not make it to his destination.
The harsh terrain and lack of resources make the journey much more difficult than he anticipated.
However, the challenges also make the cyclist more determined.
He refuses to give up, and he becomes more resourceful in finding ways to survive.
When he finally finds a bait and tackle store with water, he feels a sense of relief and confidence that he will make it to his destination safely.
The cyclist's experience shows that even in the face of adversity, one can persevere and overcome challenges.
The affect of these problems is that the biker becomes desperate, determined, and, finally, confidence and relief.

He feels like he might die from heatstroke.
The abandoned factory adds to the desperation that the cyclist feels.
The factory was once a place where people worked, but now it is abandoned.
The cyclist feels like he is alone in the world, and he is afraid that he will not make it to his destination.
The cyclist becomes more resourceful in finding ways to survive.

Whatever the reason, you might have wondered if it should be removed from the shelves.
This is a topic of much debate, and one that I have some strong opinions on.
As Katherine Paterson, the author of many beloved children's books, once said, "All of us can think of a book that we hope none of our children or any other children have taken off the shelf.

Censorship in libraries is a controversial topic.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I believe that censorship goes against our basic right to freedom of speech and expression.
Everyone should have access to information and ideas, even if they are controversial or unpopular.
Firstly, censorship limits our ability to learn and grow as individuals.
If we only have access to information that has been deemed acceptable by those in power, we will never be able to challenge our own beliefs or broaden our perspectives.
We need to be exposed to different ideas and opinions, even if we don't agree with them.
This is how we learn and develop critical thinking skills.
What one person finds offensive, another person may not.
If we start removing materials from libraries based on personal opinions, we risk limiting access to important works of literature and art.
For example, "To Kill a Mockingbird" by Harper Lee is a classic novel that has been challenged and banned in many schools and libraries.
However, this book provides important commentary on race relations and social justice.
By removing it from the shelves, we limit the ability of students to learn about these important issues.
Lastly, censorship sets a dangerous precedent.
If we start censoring books, where do we draw the line?
Who gets to decide what is offensive or inappropriate?
This could lead to a slippery slope where any material that challenges the status quo or goes against the beliefs of those in power is removed from circulation.
This is not a world that I want to live in.
In conclusion, I believe that censorship in libraries is a dangerous practice that goes against our basic human rights.
We should not remove materials from shelves simply because they are deemed offensive or inappropriate.
Instead, we should make sure that children are not exposed to materials that are not age-appropriate.
By doing this, we can preserve our right to freedom of speech and expression while also ensuring the safety of our children.

Because it had too many problems."
I laughed so hard that tears came to my eyes.
It was a good laugh, and it made me forget about my bad grade for a moment.
As we continued walking, we saw a man walking his dog.
The dog was a little Chihuahua, and it was wearing a pink sweater.
My friend and I looked at each other and started laughing.
We thought it was so funny that this little dog was wearing a sweater.
The man must have heard us because he looked back at us and smiled.
We smiled back and kept walking.
We walked a little further, and my friend slipped on a patch of ice.
She fell down, and her books went flying everywhere.
I was worried that she was hurt, but she started laughing.
She said, "I'm okay, I just need to be more careful."
I helped her gather her books, and we continued walking home.
When we got to my house, my mom was there.
She asked us how our day was, and we told her about our bad math test.
My friend told my mom the joke she had told me earlier, and my mom laughed too.
We all sat down at the kitchen table, and my mom made us hot chocolate.
We started talking and laughing, and it felt like all of our worries had disappeared.
We were just three people sitting around a table, enjoying each other's company.
That day, I learned that laughter is an important part of any relationship.
It can bring people together and make them forget about their problems, even if it's just for a little while.
My friend and I still laugh about that day, and whenever we see a dog wearing a sweater, we remember how funny it was.
Laughter is like a glue that holds people together, and I'm grateful for all the laughs I've shared with my friends and family.
Some books in libraries offend others.
This is a question that has been debated for a long time.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, magazines, etc., should be removed from the shelves if they are found offensive.
However, I believe that censorship in libraries is not necessary for several reasons.
Firstly, everyone has different tastes and preferences.
What offends one person may not offend another.
If we start removing materials that offend some people, we will end up removing everything from the shelves.
This is because someone will always find something offensive about any material.
What may be offensive to one person may not be offensive to another.
Secondly, censorship limits our freedom of expression.
It is important to have access to all kinds of materials to broaden our knowledge and understanding of the world.
If we start removing materials that are offensive, we are limiting our ability to learn about different perspectives and ideas.
Keeping people under self-control is top priorities for the public.
So why do they keep releasing and publishing books if it offends certain groups?
Graphic and gorey books are books usually that disgust people but should all contain a warning symbol on it for people with weak stomachs and those who just can't handle it.
So by that means, I'm fine with it.
People need to accept that the world is not all sunshine and rainbows and that gruesome stuff is out there.
This is my take on the whole situation.
So people, if you can't take the heat, stay out of the kitchen.
However offense material to races, religions, and other personal aquisitions, is something of different concerns.
This can certainly inflame groups, and even start protest or boycotting it.
Authors in some cases need to review their materialand make sure it won't cause any disruption.
Inflaming the public is not what you want young authors.
This can not only make the public upset, but can possibly lead to the author getting fired.
False statement or inaccurate statements in books can lead to public curiosity and even conspiracy.
Not only will it cause a stir up in the press, but just like the race/religion thing, it can cause the author to be fired.
This is not what the author wants.
So making sure the work is true and not hipotheticle is a good step.
These are great steps to achieving a positive step to public influence.
So inconclusion, authors have lots on their hands.
They need to make sure their work is accurate and won't cause any disruption.
If the book is just gory and not accurate, then it should be allowed to stay on the shelves with a warning symbol.
But if it's offensive material, then it should be reviewed and taken off the shelves if necessary.
It's important to respect everyone's beliefs and not cause any unnecessary harm.

I realized that being patient doesn't just mean waiting for things.
It means enjoying the journey, even if it takes a long time.

It brought my family closer together and created a bond that will last a lifetime.

Censorship in libraries has been a controversial topic for years.
Some people believe that certain materials, such as books, music, movies, and magazines, should be removed from the shelves if they are found to be offensive.
However, I believe that censorship is not the best solution to this problem.
In this essay, I will discuss the reasons why I believe that censorship is not the answer.
First of all, censorship limits our freedom of speech and expression.
Everyone has the right to read, watch, and listen to whatever they choose.
Censorship takes away that right and promotes a culture of fear and repression.
If we start censoring books, movies, and music, where does it end?
What will be the next thing that people will want to censor?
It is a slippery slope, and we need to be careful not to go down that path.
What one person finds offensive, another person may not.
All of us have different opinions and beliefs, and we should respect each other's right to express them.
If we start censoring materials based on one person's opinion, we are denying the rest of society the chance to make their own choices.
All of us can think of a book, movie, or song that we find offensive.
But if we start removing everything that offends someone, we will have no books, movies, or music left on the shelves.
The library would lose its purpose, and people would stop going there.
The library is a place where people can go to learn and explore new ideas.
It should be a place where people feel free to read, watch, and listen to whatever they choose.
In conclusion, I believe that censorship is not the answer to the problem of offensive materials in libraries.
We need to respect each other's right to free speech and expression.
We need to remember that censorship is subjective and impractical.
We need to focus on educating people about the importance of tolerance and respect for others.
By doing so, we can create a society that is open-minded and accepting of different ideas and perspectives.

FORGET THAT OLD SAYING ABOUT NEVER taking candy from strangers.

No, a better piece of advice for the solo cyclist would be, “Never accept travel advice from a collection of old-timers who haven’t left the confines of their porches since Carter was in office.” It’s not that a group of old guys doesn’t know the terrain.
With age comes wisdom and all that, but the world is a fluid place.
At a reservoir campground outside of Lodi, California, I enjoyed the serenity of an early-summer evening and some lively conversation with these old codgers.
What I shouldn’t have done was let them have a peek at my map.
Like a foolish youth, the next morning I followed their advice and launched out at first light along a “shortcut” that was to slice away hours from my ride to Yosemite National Park.
They’d sounded so sure of themselves when pointing out landmarks and spouting off towns I would come to along this breezy jaunt.
I rode into the morning with strong legs and a smile on my face.

About forty miles into the pedal, I arrived at the first “town.” This place might have been a thriving little spot at one time—say, before the last world war—but on that morning it fit the traditional definition of a ghost town.
I chuckled, checked my water supply, and moved on.
The sun was beginning to beat down, but I barely noticed it.
The cool pines and rushing rivers of Yosemite had my name written all over them.
Becoming dehydrated drained and weakened him physically.
Mentally, the short, rolling hills?drained him.
He had to keep convincing himself that he could make it, but seeing every hill he had to climb was discouraging.
Physically it hurt him too but more mentally, it gave him the feeling that he was going to die.
He knew that if he had taken the way he was going to take instead of the path the old men advised, that he would have been better off.
Facing rolling hills, scorching heat, and dehydration, the cyclist began to give up hope.
Twenty miles up the road, I came to a fork of sorts.
One ramshackle shed, several rusty pumps, and a corral that couldn’t hold in the lamest mule greeted me.
I had been hitting my water bottles pretty regularly, and I was traveling through the high deserts of California in June.
I got down on my hands and knees, working the handle of the rusted water pump with all my strength.
A tarlike substance oozed out, followed by brackish water feeling somewhere in the neighborhood of two hundred degrees.
I pumped that handle for several minutes, but the water wouldn’t cool down.
When I tried a drop or two, it had the flavor of battery acid.
The old guys had sworn the next town was only eighteen miles down the road.
I would conserve my water and go inward for an hour or so—a test of my inner spirit.
Not two miles into this next section of the ride, I noticed the terrain changing.
Flat road was replaced by short, rolling hills.
After I had crested the first few of these, a large highway sign jumped out at me.
It read: ROUGH ROAD AHEAD: DO NOT EXCEED POSTED SPEED LIMIT.
I was doing a water-depleting 12 mph.
Sometimes life can feel so cruel.
At some point, tumbleweeds crossed my path and a ridiculously large snake—it really did look like a diamondback—blocked the majority of the pavement in front of me.
I eased past, trying to keep my balance in my dehydrated state.
The water bottles contained only a few tantalizing sips.

Wide rings of dried sweat circled my shirt, and the growing realization that I could drop from heatstroke on a gorgeous day in June simply because I listened to some gentlemen who hadn’t been off their porch in decades, caused me to laugh.
It was a sad, hopeless laugh, mind you, but at least I still had the energy to feel sorry for myself.
There was no one in sight, not a building, car, or structure of any kind.
I began breaking the ride down into distances I could see on the horizon, telling myself that if I could make it that far, I’d be fine.
Over one long, crippling hill, a building came into view.
I wiped the sweat from my eyes to make sure it wasn’t a mirage, and tried not to get too excited.
With what I believed was my last burst of energy, I maneuvered down the hill.
In an ironic twist that should please all sadists reading this, the building—abandoned years earlier, by the looks of it—had been a Welch’s Grape Juice factory and bottling plant.
A sandblasted picture of a young boy pouring a refreshing glass of juice into his mouth could still be seen.
That smoky blues tune “Summertime” rattled around in the dry honeycombs of my deteriorating brain.
I got back on the bike, but not before I gathered up a few pebbles and stuck them in my mouth.
I’d read once that sucking on stones helps take your mind off thirst by allowing what spit you have left to circulate.
With any luck, I’d hit a bump and lodge one in my throat.
I was going to die and the birds would pick me clean, leaving only some expensive outdoor gear and a diary with the last entry in praise of old men, their wisdom, and their keen sense of direction.
I made a mental note to change that paragraph if it looked like I was going to lose consciousness for the last time.
Somehow, I climbed away from the abandoned factory of juices and dreams, slowly gaining elevation while losing hope.
Then, as easily as rounding a bend, my troubles, thirst, and fear were all behind me.
GARY AND WILBER’S FISH CAMP—IF YOU WANT BAIT FOR THE BIG ONES, WE’RE YOUR BEST BET!
“And the only bet,” I remember thinking.

As I stumbled into a rather modern bathroom and drank deeply from the sink, I had an overwhelming urge to seek out Gary and Wilber, kiss them, and buy some bait—any bait, even though I didn’t own a rod or reel.
An old guy sitting in a chair under some shade nodded in my direction.
Cool water dripped from my head as I slumped against the wall beside him.
“Where you headed in such a hurry?”   “Yosemite,” I whispered.
“Know the best way to get there?”   I watched him from the corner of my eye for a long moment.
He was even older than the group I’d listened to in Lodi.
I own a very good map.”   And I promised myself right then that I’d always stick to it in the future.

SKOPJE, Macedonia (AP) — A Macedonian court has overturned the more than decade-old terrorism convictions of 10 ethnic Albanian men, many of whom served long prison terms over a mine attack on a NATO vehicle.
The Skopje criminal ruled that there was no evidence linking the men to the 2003 blast in northern Macedonia that killed two Polish soldiers and their Macedonian translator.
The decision to overturn the convictions comes after years of legal battles and appeals by the defendants, who have always maintained their innocence.
The case has been a source of tension between Macedonia's ethnic Albanian minority and the majority Slavic population.
The court's ruling has been welcomed by human rights organizations and the defendants' families, who have long argued that the men were wrongfully convicted.
The men are now expected to be released from prison and their convictions overturned, marking a significant development in a case that has been closely watched both domestically and internationally.

I honestly think that anything should be allowed in libraries.
Libraries are supposed to be a place where people can find all kinds of information, even if it might be controversial or unpopular.
If we start censoring what people can read, watch, or listen to, then we are limiting their freedom of speech and their right to access information.
Of course, there are some materials that might be offensive or inappropriate for certain age groups.
For example, a book that contains explicit sexual content or graphic violence might not be suitable for young children.
However, I don't think that means we should ban those books altogether.
Instead, we should have different levels or sections in the library that cater to different age groups.
That way, parents can choose what their children can access, and adults can still have access to all kinds of information.
Furthermore, who gets to decide what is offensive or inappropriate?
Everyone has different values and beliefs, and what might be offensive to one person might not be to another.
If we start censoring materials based on the opinions of a few people, then we are denying everyone else the chance to make their own decisions.
In my experience, reading books that contain controversial topics or viewpoints has helped me broaden my perspective and learn about different cultures and beliefs.
I don't think that anything should ever be banned for what it says or shows or sounds like.
Instead, moved from one area to a different area.
For example, instead of showing certain things at low levels where younger people can get there hands on, they should be at a higher level or behind the desk.
